title: US to finalize sharply lower vehicle fuel economy standards
author: Reuters
description: WASHINGTON: The US Transportation Department on Monday will finalize sharply lower vehicle fuel economy standards through 2031, reversing a push by the Biden administration to force automakers to build more electric vehicles, officials said on Saturday. President Donald Trump said he had approved new fuel economy standards for cars and trucks, which he said will lower the price of new vehicles. “A major victory for America’s auto workers is coming Monday,” Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said. The new standards would cut the cost of new vehicles but increase fuel consumption and carbon dioxide emissions for decades, according to the department’s own estimates. Trump’s push comes as American drivers are grappling with sharply higher fuel prices since the start of the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran at the end of February. Under Democratic President Joe Biden, the government sought to push automakers to build more electric vehicles to meet rising fuel-efficiency standards. Biden increased required fuel efficiency for cars by 8% annually for model years 2024 and 2025, 10% for 2026 and 2% annually from 2027 to 2031. The Trump administration in December proposed retroactively revising down the 2022 model year fuel economy standard and then raising it between 0.25% and 0.5% annually through 2031. The Transportation Department proposed a fleetwide average of 34.5 miles per gallon (14.7 km per liter) by 2031, down from 50.4 miles per gallon (21.4 km per liter) under Biden. It estimated its proposal would cut average new vehicle costs by $930 each. But it would increase fuel consumption by around 100 billion gallons through 2050, fuel spending by $185 billion and carbon dioxide emissions by about 5%, the department said. Trump’s move will make it easier for automakers to sell consumers less efficient vehicles. “Lowering standards will accelerate what (Trump) has already been doing: handing the clean tech future to China and forcing Americans to pay more at the pump,” said Pete Buttigieg, who headed the Transportation Department under Biden. Biden focused on reducing US greenhouse gas emissions and fossil fuel use, accelerating a transition to clean energy and making the US. a global leader in clean-energy technology and manufacturing.

title: US consulate builder in Milan to pay $35 million over labour probe, document shows
author: Reuters
description: MILAN: US builder Caddell Construction has formally committed to pay €30.941 million ($35.24 million) in a probe into alleged worker exploitation at the site of the new US consulate in Milan, a document seen by Reuters showed. The Alabama-based construction giant undertook to pay nearly €20 million to workers in overtime, accommodation reimbursements and compensation for non-material damages, according to a document submitted by the firm to Milan prosecutors. It did not admit any liability. Caddell did not respond to a request for comment. In a statement issued in June, Caddell said it was proactively cooperating with judicial authorities and was “committed to treating and paying workers fairly”. The company specialises in large-scale projects, including contracts for US embassies and military facilities. Caddell Construction’s Italian unit was placed under investigation for alleged labour exploitation and put under judicial administration on May 29, a measure upheld by a judge two weeks later. Milan prosecutors and Italy’s Carabinieri police accused the company of recruiting workers in India through an intermediary based in New Delhi and employing them on “exhausting shifts, underpaid, without safety protections and under the constant threat of dismissal”. Iran insists on diplomatic solution after Trump rejects peace plan The company has also agreed to pay more than €7 million to Italy’s social security agency INPS and almost €4 million to the Labour Inspectorate, the document showed. In the letter to Milan prosecutors, signed by Caddell Construction executive officer Michael Angelo Ranieri and reviewed by Reuters, the US company stressed that its commitments did not amount to any admission of wrongdoing. “Furthermore, they do not imply any acceptance of the legal and factual assessments made by the authorities involved,” it added. Case against company set to be dismissed after payment Two sources with direct knowledge of the matter said the agreement involves the regularisation of around 500 workers, the recognition by the Italian state of residence permits for 270 foreign workers and unemployment benefits for 60 workers who had been dismissed. One of the two sources said that, once the payments had been made, Milan prosecutors were expected to seek the dismissal of the case against Caddell’s Italian unit. The source added that prosecutors were expected to pursue plea bargain agreements with two Caddell executives arrested as part of the investigation. Construction on the US consulate in Milan started in 2022. The contract was worth almost $210 million and work was initially scheduled to finish in 2025, but this date was subsequently put back to 2028. A US State Department spokesperson told Reuters in June that US law enforcement was cooperating with the Italian authorities, and that “the US government does not tolerate labour exploitation”. This is the latest in a series of labour exploitation investigations conducted in recent years by Milan prosecutor Paolo Storari. The probes have forced companies to grant fuller employment rights to more than 60,000 workers and enabled authorities to recover more than €1 billion ($1.1 billion), while also fuelling a heated debate over whether Italy’s judiciary is overstepping its role.

title: Iran insists on diplomatic solution after Trump rejects peace plan
author: Reuters
description: WASHINGTON/UNITED NATIONS/CAIRO: Iran on Sunday insisted that only diplomacy can solve its conflict with the United States and Israel after US President Donald Trump said he rejected an Iranian proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz and end fighting. “Our conditions are clear, and any move toward reopening the Strait of Hormuz is contingent on these conditions being met,” Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi posted on social media. “Only a negotiated solution can get them out of this deadlock.” Iran announced a peace proposal last week at the UN General Assembly in New York, saying it had been transmitted to the Americans via Qatari mediators. Trump said on Saturday he rejected the plan and argued that desperation was driving the Iranians’ push for an agreement on the key waterway. “They want to make a deal to open the Hormuz Strait immediately because they’re losing so badly,” Trump told reporters at the White House. The US has imposed an economic blockade on Iran to put pressure on Tehran to stop Iranian attacks on vessels in the Strait of Hormuz, which have drastically reduced shipping through the area even as Trump repeatedly asserts that the US controls the waterway. The Wall Street Journal first reported that Trump had rejected the Iranian proposal, citing unnamed US officials. title: Northern Ireland court allows Protestant march in Catholic area
author: Reuters
description: BELFAST: A Protestant parade may proceed through a Catholic area, Northern Ireland’s High Court ruled early on Sunday, reversing a temporary ban on the highly charged march in an area that has historically been a flashpoint of sectarian disputes. The High Court dismissed a new application to stop the Orange Order from going through the area of Portadown after the Court of Appeal vacated a temporary injunction granted on Saturday to residents who opposed the parade. Residents of the Garvaghy Road area had challenged Friday’s ruling by Northern Ireland’s Parades Commission that permitted the Orange Order to march along their road, a Catholic enclave in the largely Protestant town, overturning an almost 30-year ban on the route. A crowd gathered on the Garvaghy Road early on Sunday morning to protest against the ruling allowing the march. In the crowd were Northern Ireland First Minister Michelle O’Neill, who is also vice president of the Irish nationalist Sinn Fein party, and her party’s leader, Mary Lou McDonald, video posted on social media showed. “Although the forces of darkness may want to stop us creating a new united Ireland, they will fail,” McDonald told a crowd of protesters in the clip, posted on X. France warns UK not to ‘play’ with N Ireland Brexit deal Carla Lockhart, a member of parliament from the Democratic Unionist Party, told reporters outside the court that it was up to Sinn Fein and other nationalist politicians to abide by the rule of law and allow the parade to pass through. The original dispute over the route became one of the defining flashpoints of the conflict in Northern Ireland. Annual attempts by the Protestant Orange Order to march through the area triggered unrest across the British-run region before the route was banned in 1998, the year the Good Friday Agreement largely ended the three decades of violence known as the “Troubles”. The Parades Commission’s determination on Friday stipulated that a smaller-than-usual 35 people could take part in the march, that it should begin by 8 a.m. (0700 GMT) and finish by 9:30 a.m. and that no supporters or bands would be allowed. The commission had initially maintained its ban, but the High Court quashed that decision in August over a procedural error.

title: OpenAI, Anthropic CEOs called to appear at Australian AI probe
author: Reuters
description: SYDNEY: The CEOs of OpenAI and Anthropic have been called to appear at an Australian Senate inquiry on AI, the head of the probe said on Sunday, days after the revelation that a rogue OpenAI bot had hacked the country’s health-system database. The Medicare breach, condemned by Prime Minister Anthony Albanese , is one of the highest-profile incidents of AI agents accessing external systems outside the US. title: War in the Gulf
author: Aizaz Ahmad Chaudhry
description: The conflict has been nothing short of a disaster for the US itself.
text: THE war that the US and Israel imposed on Iran this year has failed to achieve any of the objectives that the two countries had intended. The declared purpose was to prevent Iran from building a nuclear weapon. A fact-check indicates that Iran had kept its civil nuclear programme under IAEA safeguards. It had also willingly agreed to a nuclear deal in 2015. It was President Donald Trump who pulled the US out of the deal in 2018 and re-engaged with Iran in his second term under a “maximum pressure” campaign. While talks were still underway, Israel attacked Iran in June 2025, resulting in a 12-day war. Having failed to subdue Iran, the US and Israel launched joint strikes on Iran on Feb 28, this year, killing much of the Iranian leadership and relentlessly bombing Iranian facilities and installations for 40 days. All this while Iran remained in the NPT and maintained that it was not building a nuclear bomb, thanks in large measure to a directive from Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei to not pursue a nuclear weapon programme. This means that Tehran’s nuclear programme was only a pretext to attack Iran this year. Arguably, the real objective of the February strike was to change the ruling regime in Iran. It would be recalled that by 2020, many Arab countries had joined the Abraham Accords and normalised relations with Israel. Lest the Palestinian cause be forgotten, Hamas mounted a resistance attack on Israel in October 2023, which was used by the Benjamin Netanyahu government to bomb Gaza to rubble, committing horrific genocide. Having weakened Hamas and Hezbollah, Israel began to entertain the idea of establishing a ‘Greater Israel’ and found the Iranian regime to be a major roadblock to its ambitions. Since his efforts to dislodge Iran’s government had failed in June 2025, Netanyahu persuaded Trump to undertake a joint attack against Iran on Feb 28. Two factors seem to have encouraged Trump to accept this gamble. He had successfully dislodged the government of president Nicolás Maduro in Venezuela in January, and Iran had witnessed massive protests against the government on account of inflation. The US and Israeli leadership wrongly assessed that they would be able to wipe out the Iranian regime within days. They also failed to destroy Iran’s long-range missile programme, though they did succeed in weakening Iran’s Axis of Resistance. The conflict has been nothing short of a disaster for the US itself. While Iran has survived the American and Israeli onslaught, the war has been nothing less than a disaster for the US itself. For the first time, there is a fracture in America’s relations with the Jewish state. The Gulf states are increasingly becoming disillusioned with America’s capacity or will to provide them with security. The US bases in the region have been practically destroyed. The myth of invincibility of the US military machine has been shattered. The Strait of Hormuz, which was open before the war, is now being contested. The war is expanding horizontally, with Iraqi militias targeting Saudi Arabia’s east-west pipeline and Yemen’s Houthis attacking Saudi cities and oil installations. Bab al-Mandeb also runs the risk of closure as the Houthis have captured all key positions and islands along the Red Sea. With oil prices soaring, most countries have run into serious economic difficulties. The Gulf countries, whose economies largely depended on energy flows, tourism, and services, have been shaken to the core. Meanwhile, Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkiye have entered into a regional arrangement for joint defence, predicated on the principle of collective security. With Israeli pa­­rliamentary elections due on Oct 27 and mid-term Congressional elections in Ame­rica on Nov 3, the US is contemplating how best to handle the war with Iran. One way is to revert to the MoU that was mediated by Pakistan and signed in June by the presidents of the US and Iran. However, the MoU had received severe criticism within the US and was largely interpreted as capitulation by the US. Ever since, Trump has pulled back from any peace attempts. The other option being considered is to resort to another large-scale military attack. Given what had happened in the earlier military campaigns, it can be safely assumed that another confrontation is unlikely to yield a different result. The only feasible solution is diplomacy. Pakistan, Qatar, and others must continue their efforts for peace. Secondly, it is time for China to step in as a mediator as it depends heavily on oil flows from the Gulf and had successfully brokered normalisation between Iran and Saudi Arabia in 2023. China should also impress upon the US leadership the futility of finding a military solution to the crisis in the Gulf region. The writer is chairman Sanober Institute and a former foreign secretary of Pakistan. Published in Dawn, September 27th, 2026

title: Progress at UNGA
author: Editorial
description: Any new agreement should cover all fronts: Gaza, Lebanon and Yemen.
text: ALTHOUGH no breakthrough was achieved at the UN General Assembly, there has been some progress where finding a negotiated solution to the US war on Iran is concerned. For example, both the American and Iranian delegations held talks mediated by Qatar, while the Iranian president told Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif that Tehran was still committed to the Islamabad MoU. Moreover, other reports indicate that both the US and Iran are looking for an off-ramp, with Tehran offering to open the Strait of Hormuz for marine traffic if Washington ends its blockade of Iran. The key question is: who will blink first in this battle of wits, as neither side will want to appear weak? Now it is up to both sides — as well as the states mediating this conflict — to take forward the progress made in New York. As the US, along with Israel, initiated this aggression, it should take the first step and offer confidence-building measures to Iran in order to de-escalate the situation and come to a long-term settlement. Though White House officials have said Iran is ‘desperate’ for a deal, the fact is that high fuel prices are also hurting the Trump administration at home. An unpopular war coupled with high inflation is not likely to have a positive effect on the Republicans’ chances going into November’s midterm elections. In a meeting on the UNGA sidelines, Mr Trump’s Gulf allies reportedly asked him for a post-midterm strategy regarding Iran. Perhaps something can come out of the interactions at the UN. However, the talks must not be a ruse to open Hormuz and to merely suspend hostilities and stabilise oil prices until the US midterms. There are some indications that the Trump administration may be considering kinetic action after the elections. It would mean a disastrous new confrontation in the Middle East. Hopefully, wiser counsel will prevail in Washington. The way forward seems simple. The US must approach Iran with sincerity, and the talks must not be a smokescreen for further military action later. The blockade of Iran should be lifted and its funds released to enable a longer-term peace. Tehran, on its part, should commit to keeping Hormuz open in the interest of both its neighbours and the wider international community, while also refraining from targeting the Gulf states. Also, any new agreement should cover all fronts: Gaza, Lebanon and Yemen. Although these are separate conflicts, they are also interlinked as Iranian allies are involved in all of them fighting Israel, the US and Saudi Arabia. Hence, a peace treaty with Iran alone may not last unless there is also calm in other regional theatres, while there is a particular need to rein in Israel’s murderous attacks on regional states. title: Four dialysis patients test positive for HIV at Mian Channu hospital
author: Imran Gabol
description: Infected patients, including three women, sent to Multan’s Nishtar Hospital.
text: LAHORE: Four patients undergoing dialysis at the Tehsil Headquarters Hospital (THQ), Mian Channu, have tested positive for HIV, raising fresh concerns about infection-control practices at healthcare facilities in south Punjab. According to the reports available with Dawn , the patients, including three women, who had been receiving dialysis at the hospital tested positive for the deadly virus after initial diagnosis. The hospital administration has referred them to the Nishtar Hospital Multan for further medical evaluation and treatment and they are currently under treatment there. The Mian Channu hospital officials told the media that more than 60 patients were receiving dialysis at the facility and HIV could not be transmitted through the dialysis process. They said that they were assessing the situation. Infected patients, including three women, sent to Multan’s Nishtar Hospital Sources, however, said that more dialysis patients might also have tested positive but the officials did not confirm more cases. In recent years, several HIV cases were reported in the healthcare facilities in Punjab. In November 2024, around 30 kidney patients at the Nishtar Hospital were reported to have contracted HIV during dialysis, while one patient died after developing complications. A Punjab government fact-finding committee subsequently confirmed an HIV/AIDS outbreak in the hospital’s nephrology unit and identified violations of dialysis guidelines and standard operating procedures. A scientific study published in 2026, involving researchers from the Aga Khan University and the Punjab AIDS Control Programme, found that the Multan dialysis cases were closely linked and provided evidence that the infections originated within the healthcare setting. The Punjab government ordered proceedings under the PEEDA Act against senior officials and medical staff over alleged negligence and mismanagement related to the outbreak in Nishtar Hospital Multan in January 2025. Another major HIV-related crisis had emerged in Taunsa where 106 children tested HIV positive and they were registered with the AIDS Control Programme in March 2025. The government had established a screening and treatment centre at the THQ hospital and ordered action against senior local health officials. Later, a joint mission involving WHO, Unicef, UNAIDS and other partners carried out door-to-door screening of around 50,000 people in the affected area. It also said auto-disable syringes were supplied to government hospitals and that hundreds of clinics allegedly being run by quacks were sealed. The Punjab AIDS Control Programme says it provides free HIV testing, counselling, treatment, diagnostic services and follow-up care and treatment centres were established in districts, including Lahore, Multan and Dera Ghazi Khan, and more than 14,000 patients were receiving free treatment. At the federal level, the National AIDS Control Programme says 84,421 HIV cases were registered in Pakistan by December 2025, of whom 60,785 were receiving antiretroviral therapy at 98 centres. title: Microsoft revamps Copilot with code generation
author: Reuters
description: BENGALURU: Microsoft on Friday unveiled several new capabilities in its Copilot app, including a coding tool and an always-on AI agent, as the software giant seeks to transform its AI assistant into a one-stop shop for office workers. The company is also embedding its Office applications Word, Excel, and PowerPoint directly within Copilot, allowing users to work collaboratively on these apps without having to leave the AI tool. Shares of the Redmond, Washington-based company rose about 3percent in early trading. Microsoft is racing to expand Copilot beyond its chat-based roots to boost adoption as it competes with AI chatbots such as ChatGPT and Claude. The Windows maker unveiled “Code” to let users build apps, dashboards and other software using natural language prompts. The tool, powered by the same technology as Microsoft’s GitHub Copilot, will roll out to early-access customers at the end of the month, while 365 Premium and Pro subscribers can preview it later this year. Microsoft is also rolling out “Autopilot”, a revamp of the “Scout” AI agent it unveiled in June, in a private preview at the end of the month. The so-called digital coworker agent will carry its own identity in the company directory and have specific permissions that users can control. “I think it’s been very hard for many organizations to bring agents into the enterprise because of security, compliance and governance concerns,” Annie Pearl, corporate vice president of Copilot Product, said in an interview. “So we’ve worked… to make sure that we were building this in a way that would really be able to be used in the enterprise.” Microsoft also unveiled cost-management capabilities to allow employees to have direct insight into costs tied to their AI usage. The move comes at a time when enterprises are increasingly worried about rapid AI usage racking up unexpected costs.

title: Euro zone business activity posts surprise upturn, PMI shows
author: Reuters
description: LONDON: Business activity across the euro zone accelerated this month at its fastest rate in over three years, confounding expectations for a slowdown, but firms faced a steeper rise in operating costs, a survey showed. The S&P Global Flash Euro Zone Composite PMI Output Index jumped to 53.1 in September from August’s 52.0, its highest reading since April 2023 and defying expectations in a Reuters poll for a dip to 51.7. A reading above 50.0 signals an expansion in activity. “It’s no surprise to see inflationary pressures on the rise again in September, given the increase in energy prices emanating from the ongoing conflict in the Middle East, so it’s all the more encouraging to see the resilience of economic growth being reported,” said Chris Williamson, chief business economist at S&P Global. Overall new orders surged at their fastest pace in over four years supported by a further rise in exports - which include intra-euro zone trade. Both the services and manufacturing industries contributed to the expansion. The services PMI bounced to 53.0 from 51.6, its highest in nearly a year and well ahead of the poll estimate for a fall to 51.5. The manufacturing index held steady at August’s 52.7 but a gauge of output - which feeds into the composite PMI - nudged up to 53.4 from 53.3. To meet the rise in demand firms took on more staff but faced a jump in input costs due to elevated energy prices stemming from the US war with Iran. They were able to pass some of this on to customers. Earlier this month the European Central Bank raised interest rates for the second time this year to quell an energy-driven inflation rise and warned price pressures could prove lasting. Markets are pricing three more hikes by end-June. “The resilience of economic growth amid the headwinds of geopolitical issues and rising prices will likely embolden the ECB to hike interest rates again before the end of the year, adding to the case for rates to rise sooner rather than later to put an October hike very much on the table,” Williamson added.

title: India lowers FY27 gross borrowing, to sell debt worth 7.86 tln
author: Reuters
description: MUMBAI: The Indian government plans to raise 7.86 trillion rupees (USD82 billion) through bond sales between October and March, slightly less than previously planned, as it seeks to contain rising yields and steady the market. The gross borrowing for the full financial year works out to be 16 trillion rupees (15.995 trillion rupees), down from 16.09 trillion rupees announced in the first half of the financial year and the 17.20 trillion rupees announced at the budget. New Delhi has so far raised 8.1350 trillion rupees in the April-September period, after borrowing 65 billion rupees less than planned at an auction two weeks ago. The government will sell securities maturing in three, five, seven, 15, 30, 40 and 50 years, along with the 10-year, which constitutes the largest share of borrowing. Based on wider consultation with the central bank and market feedback, the share of all four longer-duration securities has been increased, while that of the two most liquid segments - the five-year and 10-year - has seen a sharp reduction. The five-year and 10-year bonds would comprise 12.1percent and 26.3percent of the borrowings, down from 15.4percent and 29percent, respectively, in the April-September period. The 15-year and 30-year segments have seen the lion’s share of the increase in composition, with these tenors accounting for 26.8percent of supply, up from 21.8percent. Traders have said that the liquid portion of the bond yield curve could see some buying interest next week, especially after witnessing heavy selloff over the last few sessions. “Though the borrowing is not a game-changer, the composition will lead to some relief rally in the liquid five-year and 10-year segments, where any buying is much needed,” said VRC Reddy, treasury head at Karur Vysya Bank. The government will sell 150 billion rupees of green bonds in the second half, after witnessing strong demand for such notes in the April-September period. If successful, that will take the total quantum of green bonds to 300 billion rupees for the year, the highest since New Delhi started issuing such notes in fiscal ‘23. The government will sell treasury bills worth 230 billion rupees every week between October and December, a tad lower than 240 billion rupees sold on a weekly basis in the first two quarters. India’s 10-year benchmark bond yield closed at 7.1194percent on Friday, notching its sixth consecutive weekly surge.

title: OECD raises Turkey inflation forecast, trims growth outlook
author: Reuters
description: GDANSK: The Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) on Wednesday sharply raised its 2026 and 2027 inflation forecasts for Turkey, while also cutting its economic growth projections for both years. In its latest economic outlook, the OECD raised its headline inflation forecast for Turkey to 31.5percent for 2026 from 28.4percent in June, placing it above Turkish authorities’ latest projections. Its inflation projection for 2027 was also raised to 24.7percent from 18.3percent. It also cut Turkey’s economic growth forecast to 2.7percent from 3.1percent in 2026, and to 3.6percent from 3.8percent in 2027. The latest revision marks the OECD’s third downgrade of Turkey’s growth outlook this year. A large energy importer, Turkey has grappled with some of the world’s highest inflation levels in recent years, with annual inflation peaking at 85.5percent in late 2022 and surging again to above 70percent in May 2024 before starting a sustained decline following aggressive central bank tightening. While energy and fertiliser costs remain a headwind, the OECD said it expects inflation in Turkey to keep moderating, with disinflation set to continue into 2027. In June, the OECD had cut its 2026 growth forecast for Turkey, citing weaker domestic demand amid high energy and commodity prices and tighter financial conditions, while leaving its 2027 growth outlook unchanged. The revisions come as the OECD slightly raised its global growth forecasts for this year, saying AI-driven investment is helping the world economy hold up better than expected, even as a more entrenched energy shock weighs on the outlook for 2027.

title: Indonesia govt commits to cooperative loan repayments
author: Reuters
description: JAKARTA: Indonesia’s government will make repayments of bank loans that are funding a national village cooperative programme, the finance minister said, as the first instalment falls due on Friday. Suahasil Nazara, who was appointed as finance minister last week, said late on Thursday that the repayments will be made once the government verifies the funds were used as intended, including for the construction of cooperative stores in thousands of villages. “This has been budgeted, the fund is ready, we will definitely pay,” Suahasil said, noting 37 trillion rupiah (USD2.1 billion) had been allocated in the 2026 budget. “There must be verification for what have been built and how many,” he said. “There’s a validation process.” The bank loans are part of a complicated financing scheme for the “Red and White” village cooperative programme, an initiative of President Prabowo Subianto to stimulate rural economies as part of his drive to lift national growth to 8percent. Prabowo has said he wants the cooperatives to sell government-subsidised products, such as fertilisers and cooking gas, buy local produce, and offer cheap loans to villagers. FOUR STATE BANKS LEND USD13.6 BILLION Under the scheme, state company PT Agrinas Pangan Nusantara is building 80,000 stores in villages across the vast archipelago, funded by 240 trillion rupiah of low-interest loanswith 6-year tenures from four state banks. Bank Rakyat Indonesia, Bank Negara Indonesia , Bank Mandiri and Bank Syariah Indonesia are the lenders. When construction is completed, the loans will then be repaid by the government, rather than Agrinas Pangan, and eventually ownership of the cooperatives will be transferred to local communities. The Cooperative Ministry and state auditors are in charge of the verification process.

title: Closing the gap, from the bottom
author: Unknown
description: EDITORIAL: Pakistan’s strongest annual improvement in gender parity in a decade would ordinarily be cause for satisfaction. The challenge, however, is knowing quite what to celebrate when the country still ranks third-last in the World Economic Forum’s Global Gender Gap Report 2026 . Its overall gender parity score rose to 59.5 percent in 2026, almost three percentage points higher than last year and 5.2 percentage points above its 2006 score of 54.3 percent. Progress should certainly be acknowledged. But when Pakistan remains the lowest-ranked of the 38 lower-middle-income economies and all seven South Asian countries covered by the report, improvement mostly illustrates how desperately far there remains to go. The economic numbers are particularly dismal. Pakistan ranks 144th in economic participation and opportunity, even after moving up three places. Labour-force participation stands at 81.46 percent for men and just 28.21 percent for women. Women account for only 6.13 percent of legislators, senior officials and managers in the workforce, while just 3.4 percent of firms have female top managers. These figures describe an economy that continues to leave an enormous share of its human capital underutilised, an extravagance Pakistan can scarcely afford, given its persistent struggle to generate investment, productivity and sustainable growth. Education offers the most encouraging part of the report and was the principal driver of this year’s improvement. Pakistan rose substantially in educational attainment and achieved high parity in tertiary enrolment, with female and male enrolment rates reported at 10.71 and 11.01 percent, respectively. Yet the broader picture remains deeply troubling. Female literacy stands at 48.52 percent against 69.14 percent for males, while participation at both primary and secondary levels remains low. Near-parity between boys and girls becomes considerably less impressive when too many children of both sexes remain outside or fall away from the education system. The political picture is hardly reassuring either. Women comprise 21.69 percent of parliamentarians but only 3.45 percent of those holding ministerial positions, according to the report. Pakistan ranks 107th in political empowerment. Beneath representation lies the more fundamental question of rights. The WEF report highlights unequal inheritance rights for widows and daughters, restricted access to justice, and unequal divorce rights. Gender disparity therefore follows women from the household and workplace into the legal, financial and political structures that determine their ability to exercise meaningful economic and social independence. This is where incremental improvement must be kept in perspective. Moving upwards from an exceptionally low base matters because every improvement in education, employment or representation affects real lives. But celebrating movement in the rankings without confronting the underlying scale of exclusion would be dangerously complacent. A country cannot seriously pursue higher productivity while most women remain outside the labour force, nor can educational gains deliver their full economic return if qualified women encounter barriers when they attempt to enter employment or advance into senior positions. The response consequently has to extend across education, employment, law and enforcement. Keeping girls in school, improving female literacy, creating safer workplaces and transport, expanding access to finance and ensuring that legal rights exist in practice as well as on paper are interconnected parts of the same challenge. Employers and government institutions must also examine why women remain so dramatically underrepresented in positions of authority. Pakistan has improved, and that deserves recognition. But third-last is a rather uncomfortable place from which to take a victory lap. Copyright Business Recorder, 2026

title: Drill now, drown later
author: Unknown
description: EDITORIAL: UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres’ accusation that Big Oil has treated the atmosphere as an “open sewer” may be unusually blunt diplomatic language, but the underlying charge is becoming increasingly difficult to dismiss. His comparison is particularly striking at a time when the consequences of global warming are becoming harder to separate from everyday economic life. Yet the international effort to reduce dependence on fossil fuels has simultaneously encountered a powerful reversal, led by a US administration that has quite literally made “drill, baby, drill” part of its governing philosophy. That reversal matters far beyond the United States. Washington has withdrawn from the Paris Agreement, reopened vast areas to oil and gas development, accelerated drilling approvals and explicitly made expanded fossil-fuel production part of its energy strategy. Whatever progress developed economies had begun making towards a cleaner energy transition is inevitably harder to sustain when the world’s largest economy is using its political and economic weight to move forcefully in the opposite direction. The signal to producers and investors is equally important: fossil fuels have acquired a powerful new political sponsor just when climate science is demanding faster movement away from them. Guterres also draws attention to the uncomfortable economics of the climate crisis. According to the figures he cited, five major Western oil companies have accumulated nearly half a trillion dollars in profits since Russia invaded Ukraine, while only $34 billion has been mobilised to help developing countries adapt to a warming planet. That disparity goes directly to the unresolved question of climate justice. Countries with the least fiscal space to protect themselves from extreme weather are frequently those that contributed the least to creating the problem. Pakistan sits painfully close to the centre of that contradiction. Its contribution to global greenhouse-gas emissions remains below one percent, yet its exposure to floods, extreme heat, drought, glacial instability and other climate-related hazards is severe. The country has already discovered that a small carbon footprint provides no protection when the climate system responds to cumulative global emissions. Nor does moral responsibility pay for destroyed homes, damaged crops, disrupted infrastructure or the enormous cost of building resilience against the next disaster. There is, however, an awkward reality that Pakistan cannot escape either. Its economy remains dependent on fossil fuels, directly and indirectly, while energy security and affordability remain persistent constraints on growth. Developing countries cannot simply switch off conventional energy sources because wealthier economies have spent generations using them to industrialise. A disorderly transition would impose costs that Pakistan, already struggling with fiscal and external vulnerabilities, is poorly equipped to absorb. That makes the climate argument more complicated; but also more urgent. Pakistan must accelerate renewable energy, improve energy efficiency and reduce unnecessary dependence on imported fuels wherever economically feasible. At the same time, developed economies that accumulated prosperity during the fossil-fuel era have a much greater responsibility to finance adaptation and help poorer countries make the transition without sacrificing development. Climate finance cannot remain the ceremonial accompaniment to increasingly alarming climate conferences. Guterres is therefore right to direct attention towards both the polluters and the profits. The world already knows where continued dependence on fossil fuels is leading. What remains uncertain is whether governments possess the political will to change direction before adaptation itself becomes prohibitively expensive. For countries such as Pakistan, “drill, baby, drill” slogan carries a particularly grim footnote: somebody else may drill, but everybody gets the climate. Copyright Business Recorder, 2026

Whatever progress developed economies had begun making towards a cleaner energy transition is inevitably harder to sustain when the world’s largest economy is using its political and economic weight to move forcefully in the opposite direction. The signal to producers and investors is equally important: fossil fuels have acquired a powerful new political sponsor just when climate science is demanding faster movement away from them. Guterres also draws attention to the uncomfortable economics of the climate crisis. According to the figures he cited, five major Western oil companies have accumulated nearly half a trillion dollars in profits since Russia invaded Ukraine, while only $34 billion has been mobilised to help developing countries adapt to a warming planet. That disparity goes directly to the unresolved question of climate justice. Countries with the least fiscal space to protect themselves from extreme weather are frequently those that contributed the least to creating the problem. Pakistan sits painfully close to the centre of that contradiction. Its contribution to global greenhouse-gas emissions remains below one percent, yet its exposure to floods, extreme heat, drought, glacial instability and other climate-related hazards is severe. The country has already discovered that a small carbon footprint provides no protection when the climate system responds to cumulative global emissions. Nor does moral responsibility pay for destroyed homes, damaged crops, disrupted infrastructure or the enormous cost of building resilience against the next disaster. There is, however, an awkward reality that Pakistan cannot escape either. Its economy remains dependent on fossil fuels, directly and indirectly, while energy security and affordability remain persistent constraints on growth. Developing countries cannot simply switch off conventional energy sources because wealthier economies have spent generations using them to industrialise. A disorderly transition would impose costs that Pakistan, already struggling with fiscal and external vulnerabilities, is poorly equipped to absorb. That makes the climate argument more complicated; but also more urgent. Pakistan must accelerate renewable energy, improve energy efficiency and reduce unnecessary dependence on imported fuels wherever economically feasible. At the same time, developed economies that accumulated prosperity during the fossil-fuel era have a much greater responsibility to finance adaptation and help poorer countries make the transition without sacrificing development. Climate finance cannot remain the ceremonial accompaniment to increasingly alarming climate conferences. Guterres is therefore right to direct attention towards both the polluters and the profits. The world already knows where continued dependence on fossil fuels is leading. What remains uncertain is whether governments possess the political will to change direction before adaptation itself becomes prohibitively expensive. For countries such as Pakistan, “drill, baby, drill” slogan carries a particularly grim footnote: somebody else may drill, but everybody gets the climate. Copyright Business Recorder, 2026

title: Suicide blast targeting DI Khan checkpost claims 12 lives, injures 30
author: Muhammad Irfan Mughal
description: Officials say attacker rammed explosives-laden tractor trolley into checkpost; 2 killed as ambulance transporting victims comes under fire; Kundi calls on PTI to put differences aside and call off long march.
text: DERA ISMAIL KHAN: A dozen people lost their lives while 35 others were injured on Saturday when a vehicle laden with explosives was rammed into the Aman Mela police checkpost in Dera Ismail Khan’s Darazinda tehsil, officials said. Separately, two rescue workers were killed and another was injured when a Rescue 1122 ambulance came under fire while transporting bodies of victims from the blast. DI Khan Regional Police Officer (RPO) Ghulam Mubashir Maken, citing an initial assessment, confirmed the casualties from the blast. He clarified that no law enforcement or security personnel were among the deceased, which included a Customs official and civilians. The deceased comprised nine men, two women and a minor. According to police and Rescue 1122 officials, an unidentified attacker rammed the explosives-laden tractor trolley into the checkpost. DI Khan District Police Officer (DPO) Ziauddin Ahmed confirmed that it was a suicide blast. The blast destroyed a large portion of the checkpost and completely demolished a house adjacent to the post. The intensity of the explosion was such that it was heard over a considerable distance, according to local officials and residents. Heavy firing was also heard following the blast. The Aman Mela checkpost, located near Mughal Kot and Darazinda on the DI Khan-Quetta Road, is used by police for security and checking along the route. It is situated close to the border between Khyber Pakhtunkhwa and Balochistan. According to RPO Maken, 25 of the injured were taken to the district headquarters (DHQ) hospital. Meanwhile, District Excise Officer Faheem Wazir said Excise personnel present at the checkpost remained safe. A bomb disposal team was also sent to the site to determine the nature of the explosion and examine the scene, police said. DPO Ahmed and the superintendent of police for the Saddar area had reached the site soon after the explosion and supervised the rescue operation. A Rescue 1122 spokesperson noted that their teams were on the site for relief operations, but mobile phone services were unavailable in the area. Later in the day, a Rescue 1122 spokesperson said the search, recovery and relief operation at the site had been completed. More than 25 personnel, six ambulances and a fire vehicle took part in the relief operations, according to the rescue service. On the directions of District Emergency Officer (DEO) Mohammad Arif Khan, four additional ambulances with staff were dispatched from DI Khan to assist in evacuating the injured. Rescue 1122 said two of its workers were killed while another was seriously injured when an ambulance transporting some bodies recovered from the blast site was targeted by unidentified assailants near Aman Mela. The deceased rescue workers were identified as Sharifullah and Imtiaz, while Anees sustained injuries in the firing, according to a Rescue 1122 spokesperson. The injured worker was provided immediate medical treatment and taken to a hospital. Despite the firing incident, rescue teams had continued the operation to transport the bodies and assist those affected by the blast. State broadcaster Radio Pakistan attributed the attack to Fitna al Khawarij, a term the state uses to refer to the banned Tehreek-i-Taliban Pakistan (TTP). The report added that an operation by the security forces against the terrorists was underway. Chief Minister Sohail Afridi, in a video statement , condemned the attack and highlighted the funds allocated for police in KP’s budget. He also once again called for a “policy shift” on the federal government’s part regarding counterterrorism. Meanwhile, KP Governor Faisal Karim Kundi sought a report from senior officials on the incident and directed that every possible medical facility be provided to those injured. “The attack is a nefarious conspiracy by Fitna al-Hindustan Khawarij ,” the governor said. The state refers to designated Balochistan-based groups as Fitna al Hindustan to highlight India’s role in terrorism and destabilisation across Pakistan. In the wake of the blast, Kundi also requested the PTI to call off its march to Islamabad planned for Oct 4. Tagging CM Afridi’s X account, he wrote: “For the sake of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa and our people, let us put political differences aside and stand together as one. “Our people are paying the price in blood. They deserve solidarity, security and leadership focused on protecting their lives.” In an earlier post on X, Kundi said, “At a time when KP is mourning, political priorities must reflect the pain of our people.” He asserted that the provincial government “must take responsibility and put the security and lives of our people at the centre of its priorities”. “They do not need test matches or long marches. They need peace.” President Asif Ali Zardari strongly condemned the blast in a statement issued by the Presidency and expressed grief over the lives lost. The president ordered that the best medical facilities be provided to the injured, and that relief operations be made “more effective”. “Making innocent citizens and law enforcement personnel a target of terrorism is highly condemnable,” he was quoted as saying. “Operations against terrorists belonging to Fitna al Hindustan and Fitna al Khawarij , who perpetrate heinous acts with foreign support, must be made more effective.” Denouncing the attack, Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif expressed sorrow over the loss of precious human lives. He said the sacrifices of the nation’s guardians in the war against terrorism “will never be allowed to go in vain”. “The government is determined to completely eradicate terrorism from the country,” he was quoted as saying. In a statement issued by his ministry, Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi also strongly condemned the “suicide blast at the anti-smuggling Aman Mela police checkpost” and expressed his condolences to the bereaved families. “The cowardly acts of kharjis cannot weaken the nation’s firm resolve against terrorism,” he was quoted as saying, using a term the state employs to designate terrorists. “Khyber Pakhtunkhwa is on the front lines of the fight against terrorism.” Naqvi noted that people from all walks of life have made sacrifices against terrorism, adding that the state deeply values the sacrifices of martyrs. PPP Chairman Bilawal Bhutto-Zardari said that the “terrorist attack” in DI Khan, following the recent bloodshed in Kohat, was “another painful reminder of the terrorism threat Pakistan continues to confront”. “My deepest condolences to the families of our martyrs and prayers for the injured. The nation stands firmly with our courageous police, law-enforcement agencies and security forces,” he said. “Pakistan has defeated terrorism before, and we will defeat it again. Terrorists, their facilitators, financiers and sponsors will be held accountable and no territory beyond our borders will be allowed to serve as a sanctuary for terrorism against Pakistan,” he said. “We will neither be intimidated nor divided. Pakistan will prevail,” Bilawal said. Finance Minister Muhammad Aurangzeb also condemned the blast at the “Customs joint check post”. KP has witnessed an increase in terrorist activity in recent months, with law enforcement agencies and security forces being targeted, prompting authorities to intensify counterterrorism operations. Earlier this month, police said they foiled an attack by TTP terrorists on a checkpost in DI Khan’s Daraban area. No casualties were reported among the police personnel. On Sept 18, a major attack in the old Police Lines in KP’s Kohat claimed 23 lives and injured about 100 others. Eight terrorists were killed during an overnight clearance operation . In response to that and other terrorist incidents, Pakistan days later conducted “calibrated” airstrikes in the border region with Afghanistan against terrorist hideouts, with the government saying over 28 terrorists were eliminated. Mainland KP, excluding the merged districts, recorded 54 terrorist attacks in August compared with 36 in July, representing an increase of 50 per cent, according to monthly data compiled by the Pakistan Institute for Conflict and Security Studies (PICSS).

title: Discussions on terrorism
author: Ahmed Bilal Mehboob
description: We need committees that are more active in debating national security.
text: WHILE visiting the British parliament a few years ago, I was struck by the tradition —observed by prime ministers — of paying homage and expressing gratitude at the start of the weekly question time session to British armed forces personnel who had been killed or injured in action. It was the time of the Afghan war and British troops were stationed in Afghanistan. I thought it was a great tradition that reminded everyone of the sacrifices made by the soldiers and sent a powerful message to the troops that their countrymen had the highest regard for them and their sacrifices. Although Pakistan follows the British parliamentary system, almost all Pakistani prime ministers have avoided personally answering questions in parliament. As prime minister, Yousuf Raza Gilani used to answer many supplementary questions himself when he was in the House — but that was not a part of the set parliamentary procedure. Imran Khan had promised to follow this British tradition when he was prime minister and personally answer questions. However, he neither tried to change the parliamentary rules nor did he ever answer any questions in parliament. Both Houses and the provincial assemblies observe question hour but there is no parliamentary tradition of routinely acknowledging the sacrifices of the country’s shuhda and ghazis. The president, prime minister, ministers and senior civil and military officers do issue statements, and legislatures occasionally pass resolutions honouring those fighting a bloody war against terrorism; but the possibility of a weekly tribute did cross my mind. After all, hardly a day passes without hearing of security personnel — in the armed forces, paramilitaries, police and other security bodies — who have lost their lives in the line of duty. We need committees that are more active in debating national security. Almost all sources of information show that the number of violent terrorist incidents, casualties and fatalities in Pakistan have reached their highest level in a decade. In fact, 2025 was the bloodiest year since 2014. According to the South Asian Terrorism Portal, the number of violent terrorist incidents in 2025 was 1,077 with fatalities among the forces and civilians touching 1,229 and 655 respectively during the year. The data gathered for 2026 points to even higher figures when compared to the average monthly figures for 2025. For example, the number of terrorism incidents increased to a monthly average of 118, compared to 90 in 2025. Similarly, average monthly fatalities of civilian and security forces personnel in the first nine months of 2026 (up to Sept 21) have increased to 74 from 55 last year and to 114 from 102, respectively. These figures indicate a steep spike in attacks, particularly carried out by two major terrorist groups that the state aptly refers to as Fitna al-Khawarij and Fitna al-Hindustan. We do not see the level of concern and debate within democratic institutions that is warranted by the rise in acts of terrorism. We have four key standing committees relating to the issue in parliament — separate Senate and National Assembly standing committees on defence and two other committees of the Senate and National Assembly on the interior. In addition, each of the four provincial assemblies has a standing committee on home affairs. Whatever little record is available on these legislatures’ official websites does not indicate that the committees have been often and actively debating the rising incidence of terrorism in the country — especially in KP and Balochistan —in detail, which should have been done in view of the situation. The plenaries of the six national and provincial legislatures have debated the issue on and off, and passed resolutions too. I am sure that more frequent discussions in the legislative bodies would not only contribute to finding more effective ways in which the menace of terrorism can be combated at the people’s level, but the attention given by the legislators to this issue would further boost security personnel’s morale. In 2019, the Speaker of the National Assembly had constituted a joint (National Assembly and Senate) committee on national security under his own chairmanship and included the senior-most parliamentarians and ministers. But since the last election in 2024, the committee has apparently ceased to exist. It doesn’t necessarily mean that we need a parliamentary committee on national security while the committees on defence and interior already exist. However, what we need are committees that are more active in debating national security. The public should be confident that national security issues are being discussed and timely decisions being made at the appropriate forum. In this context, it is difficult to understand the relatively inactive state of the National Security Committee, which was created in 2013. The Committee, which brings together the top civil and military leadership under the chairmanship of the prime minister, has not met even once during the current calendar year. Given the prevailing circumstances and the mandate of the NSC, it should meet more regularly, preferably on a monthly basis. Just for comparison, Britain’s National Security Council meets every week under the prime minister although the UK has far fewer security issues than Pakistan. It is hoped that the National Counter Terrorism Authority — a very important body especially in the present context — will not only become more active under its new national coordinator Maj-Gen Faisal Naseer but will also attempt to raise its public profile by, for example, sharing at least a sanitised version of the progress on the implementation of the National Action Plan with the people, their representatives and the media. Extending its outreach will bolster public trust. The writer is president of the Pakistan-based think tank Pildat. Published in Dawn, September 26th, 2026

title: Info ministry dismisses Afghan claims of destroying Pakistani post near border in Balochistan as 'fake'
author: News Desk
description: Says 13 Afghan Taliban personnel killed, several injured in its retaliatory action in Gulistan sector last night.
text: The information ministry dismissed on Friday claims by the Afghan defence ministry of a Pakistani post having been destroyed near the Spin Boldak border — the frontier between Balochistan and Kandahar — as “fake and fabricated”. The information ministry also took note of Afghan claims that there had been no casualties among the Afghan forces in the latest episode of clash between the two sides. “The claim is fake and fabricated. As per actual facts, an attempted Afghan aggression in the Gulistan sector was thwarted on night between Sept 24 and Sept 25, and during the process and subsequent heavy punishment inflicted on opposing Taliban posts, at least 13 Afghan Taliban personnel were killed and several injured,” the information ministry said in a post on X. It also shared visuals in the post, which the ministry said were of the incident. The incident, it added, had already been “widely covered by media and circulated extensively across social media, providing visual evidence of the border engagement and punishment inflicted on the Afghan Taliban after their cowardly attack”. “The […] Afghan ministry’s attempt is no surprise since the Taliban are habitual liars having no moral and reputational standing,” it added. The latest clash has taken place amid an uptick in tensions at the Pak-Afghan border. Pakistan conducted precision aerial and drone strikes in 10 locations across Afghanistan on Thursday in retaliation for drones launched from the neighbouring country a day earlier. The response came after eight drones, launched from Afghanistan, entered Pakistani airspace near the Torkham border and Kohat on Wednesday. Security sources said they were subsequently shot down. It was also reported that the Afghan Taliban engaged in unprovoked firing the night before near Kurram as security forces foiled an attempt by terrorists to cross into Pakistan. On Sept 21, Pakistan, in response to recent terrorist attacks in KP, conducted “calibrated” airstrikes in the border region with Afghanistan against terrorist hideouts and safe havens of terrorist organisations. A statement from the information ministry on Monday said that over 28 terrorists were eliminated in the strikes. “It is a matter of grave concern that Afghanistan continues to remain a hub of terrorism,” the ministry said at the time, specifying that the “threat to Pakistan emanates from Afghanistan”. The airstrikes had come after a major attack in the old Police Lines in KP’s Kohat claimed 23 lives and injured about 100 others. Eight terrorists were killed during an overnight clearance operation launched to clear the area. Information Minister Attaullah Tarar described Monday’s action as part of Pakistan’s ongoing counter-terrorism campaign, Ghazab lil Haq. On the night of February 26, following unprovoked firing by the Afghan Taliban from across the border, Pakistan launched Operation Ghazab lil Haq against terrorist hideouts. Pakistan also carried out strikes in the border region with Afghanistan in late June , with the government saying they were in response to a wave of terrorist attacks, including one on a Rangers camp in Karachi . At the time, Tarar said that 25 terrorists were killed in those strikes in Paktia, Paktika and Kunar. Pakistan had carried out similar strikes on terrorist hideouts along its border with Afghanistan earlier that month, killing 26 terrorists. In July, security forces responded to unprovoked firing by the Afghan Taliban at border posts in Kurram, security sources had said. In the same month, the Afghan Taliban regime launched four rudimentary drones across the border into Balochistan, which were shot down by security forces. Two drones were also shot down in June in Qila Abdullah and Chagai districts. As clashes continue, tensions between Islamabad and Kabul have remained high. Islamabad has repeatedly urged the Taliban administration in Kabul to dismantle terrorist sanctuaries on Afghan soil, particularly those linked to the banned TTP, that are used for attacks in Pakistan. Officials say those appeals have gone unheeded. Earlier this week, Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar addressed a meeting of the Organisation of Islamic Cooperation (OIC), where he called for steps towards concrete and verifiable action to prevent the use of Afghan soil for terrorism against any neighbouring country, particularly Pakistan. Dar said Pakistan was “seriously concerned” about the presence of over two dozen terrorist groups in Afghanistan that threatened regional and international peace and security. Last week, Pakistan also told the UN Security Council that it would respond to terrorist threats emanating from Afghanistan in self-defence as and when needed and in accordance with international law. Earlier this month, the Foreign Office (FO) declared that meaningful progress in relations with Kabul would depend on the Taliban taking concrete and verifiable action against Tehreek-i-Taliban Pakistan (TTP) and other terrorist groups operating from Afghan territory. It maintained that while Islamabad welcomed China’s continuing engagement, the external facilitation could not substitute for action by Kabul against terrorist infrastructure. According to a UN Security Council-mandated monitoring report — covering the period from December 16, 2025 to June 9, 2026 — Afg­han Taliban’s continued support for TTP has contributed to a rise in the frequency and lethality of terrorist attacks in Pakistan, even as Kabul has taken some initial steps to rein in the group. The report also pointed to growing operational and facilitation linkages among the TTP, Al Qaeda, Islamic State-Khorasan (ISIL-K) and the Baloch Liberation Army (BLA).

title: Dangerous border
author: Editorial
description: Until this fundamental issue is addressed, bilateral ties will not improve.
text: WITH no let-up in terrorist attacks on Pakistan by elements finding refuge in Afghanistan, Islamabad has again launched kinetic action in the border area to target terrorist groups. The actions have resulted in exchanges of fire with the Afghan Taliban regime. Pakistan seems to be trapped in a cycle of escalation for the simple reason that Kabul is unwilling to act against terrorist groups active on its soil, such as the banned TTP, that seek to harm this country. Until this fundamental issue is addressed, bilateral ties will not improve. It was reported on Wednesday that the military had shot down drones apparently originating from Afghanistan as they attempted to violate Pakistani airspace. Earlier, Pakistan had launched air strikes in the border area, which killed a number of terrorists, after a spate of violent attacks, including the assault targeting the old Police Lines in Kohat last week. Pakistani forces also thwarted infiltration attempts in the Kurram area, which resulted in an exchange of fire with the Afghan Taliban. Along with taking kinetic action, Pakistan has highlighted this grim situation on the world stage. The UN Security Council has condemned the Kohat terrorist attack, calling for the “perpetrators … and sponsors” of the atrocity to be brought to justice. Pakistan had earlier told the UNSC that it would respond to threats originating from Afghanistan in self-defence. Moreover, the deputy prime minister, while speaking at a meeting of the OIC contact group on Afghanistan on the sidelines of the ongoing UN General Assembly session, reiterated the need for a verifiable mechanism to prevent the use of Afghan soil for terrorism. China, as well as Muslim states such as Saudi Arabia and Qatar, has backed diplomatic efforts to resolve the differences between Kabul and Islamabad. While hostilities are undesirable, if the Afghan Taliban take no action against those who spill innocent blood in this country, Pakistan will have no option but to take action to defend itself against terrorism. Yet while immediate threats must be confronted, long-term peace can only come through dialogue, and a commitment by the Taliban to curb cross-border terrorism. As has been highlighted in these columns previously, a bevy of terrorist groups call Afghanistan home, and pose a threat to the whole region, not just Pakistan — although this country, owing to its physical proximity, has been hit the hardest. Therefore, only a sustained and coordinated regional effort can succeed in eliminating the terrorist threat emanating from Afghanistan. It is clear that, ultimately, the Taliban must decide whether they want to integrate with the rest of the region, or remain a pariah regime because of their stubborn ideological attachment to their violent comrades. Two drones were also shot down in June in Qila Abdullah and Chagai districts. As clashes continue, tensions between Islamabad and Kabul have remained high. Islamabad has repeatedly urged the Taliban administration in Kabul to dismantle terrorist sanctuaries on Afghan soil, particularly those linked to the banned TTP, that are used for attacks in Pakistan. Officials say those appeals have gone unheeded. Earlier this week, Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar addressed a meeting of the Organisation of Islamic Cooperation (OIC), where he called for steps towards concrete and verifiable action to prevent the use of Afghan soil for terrorism against any neighbouring country, particularly Pakistan. Dar said Pakistan was “seriously concerned” about the presence of over two dozen terrorist groups in Afghanistan that threatened regional and international peace and security. Last week, Pakistan also told the UN Security Council that it would respond to terrorist threats emanating from Afghanistan in self-defence as and when needed and in accordance with international law. Earlier this month, the Foreign Office (FO) declared that meaningful progress in relations with Kabul would depend on the Taliban taking concrete and verifiable action against Tehreek-i-Taliban Pakistan (TTP) and other terrorist groups operating from Afghan territory. It maintained that while Islamabad welcomed China’s continuing engagement, the external facilitation could not substitute for action by Kabul against terrorist infrastructure. According to a UN Security Council-mandated monitoring report — covering the period from December 16, 2025 to June 9, 2026 — Afg­han Taliban’s continued support for TTP has contributed to a rise in the frequency and lethality of terrorist attacks in Pakistan, even as Kabul has taken some initial steps to rein in the group. The report also pointed to growing operational and facilitation linkages among the TTP, Al Qaeda, Islamic State-Khorasan (ISIL-K) and the Baloch Liberation Army (BLA).

title: Govt minimises commercial banks' role in pension payments
author: Khaleeq Kiani
description: Revised SOPs issued by finance ministry direct that pension accounts cannot be deemed dormant.
text: ISLAMABAD: The finance ministry on Monday eliminated the administrative role of commercial banks in the biometric verification and validation of proof-of-life certificates (PoLCs), in a move aimed at facilitating pensioners. The government also directed that pensioners’ bank accounts would not be subject to account dormancy requirements. The Ministry of Finance issued revised standard operating procedures (SOPs) to enable digital proof-of-life certificates (PoLCs) and pension disbursements on the directives of Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif. “The federal government has formally eliminated the role of commercial banks in carrying out standard banking biometric verification or PoLC validation for pensioners,” the finance ministry said in its notification. Instead, the National Database and Registration Authority (Nadra) has been integrated with the Controller General of Accounts (CGA) and Military Accountant General (MAG) via a secure application programming interface (API). “The Digital Life Signal is transmitted directly from Nadra to CGA/MAG, bypassing commercial banking channels,” the notification said. It added that under the new SOPs, commercial banks would serve solely as “pension disbursement agencies” and would have no statutory or administrative role in the verification, collection, retention or validation of PoLCs or biometric data under ordinary circumstances. The only exception would be when they act strictly as an authorised operational conduit through Nadra’s designated system for generating PoLCs. “Furthermore, no pension-disbursing account of a pensioner shall be rendered dormant by the bank for the purpose of processing or disbursing pension payments,” the notification declared, adding that these SOPs superseded all previous SOPs. It also formally abolished the physical “Disburser’s Half” process — paper documentation previously used for pension payments. Federal pensions will now be disbursed exclusively through the Direct Credit System (DCS). The revised SOPs were developed in consultation with all stakeholders, including the State Bank of Pakistan, Accountant General Offices, Nadra and the finance ministry, to facilitate pensioners through a more convenient mechanism while strengthening verification. The notification explained that pensioners’ accounts would no longer be marked as dormant, as already decided last month, for the purposes of the Federal Government Receipt and Payment Rules, 2025. “Standard bank dormancy requirements are non-applicable to pension accounts,” the order said. To enable the revised digital verification mechanism, pensioners would be able to complete PoLC verification via the Nadra PakID mobile app or authorised Nadra channels like Nadra Registration Centers, Mobile Units, e-Sahulat franchises or bank branches operating strictly as Nadra PoLC centers. However, the pensioners would have to ensure biannual verification. “Verification must occur at least once every six months or 180 days,” replacing the existing system of a bi-annual schedule fixed for March and September. “Pensioners may verify at any time within the 180-day interval”, it explained. Family pensioners drawing pensions, subject to marital status conditions, must submit Form-12 declarations as required. The notification said account transfers must be routed through the target scheduled bank, while overpayments or discrepancies must be reported directly to the relevant accounts office and the bank. The SOPs also provided two options for activating dormant pensioners’ accounts: either undergoing biometric verification through Nadra’s system hosted at bank branches serving as PoLC verification centres, or receiving a pension credit from the CGA/MAG from September 2026 onwards. Pension rolls will be generated by the 24th and verified by the 26th of each month for execution through the SBP’s RAAST or other micropayment channels. This will be subject to quarterly audits and reconciliation of Nadra logs. The ministry has also directed banks to open pensioners’ accounts solely in the name of the pensioner or eligible family pensioner, prohibiting joint accounts. Banks are not allowed to collect, retain, accept or verify physical life certificates or pensioners’ biometric data in their ordinary banking capacity for pension accounts. Banks also cannot compel pensioners to visit branches for biometric verification of pension accounts for standard PoLC purposes. On the other hand, if a pensioner approaches a branch with paper documentation, the bank shall direct them to the Nadra Pak-ID app or a designated Nadra registration centre and shall not collect, retain or process such documentation. Under no circumstances can a bank place a pension account on dormant status, for the purposes of the Federal Government Receipt and Payment Rules, 2025. “Banks shall not impose debit restrictions due to non-submission of proof of life to the bank.” The banks have been directed to reactivate accounts marked dormant before August 22, 2026, either following Nadra verification at an authorised branch conduit or upon confirmation of pension receipt from CGA/MAG from September 2026 onwards. Moreover, if an account was placed in ‘suspense status’ by CGA/MAG and funds remained uncollected, banks would remit the funds to the government upon receipt of formal notice from the CGA. Banks shall not independently suspend or close accounts. For pensioners unable to use the Pak-ID mobile app due to lack of digital access, advanced age or debilitating medical conditions, or in family pension cases where real-time data regarding remarriage or marital status has not been updated in Nadra records, individuals may visit a designated District Accounts Office or Pension Facilitation Centre under CGA/MAG to submit a manual life certificate (Form 10) or declaration (Form 12) regarding remarriage or marital status. In such cases, authorised personnel would upload the documents directly into the centralised system, and “commercial banks are strictly prohibited from accepting or processing Form 10 or Form 12 directly”, the notification said. Finally, quarterly reconciliations shall be carried out between accounts offices and banks based on API logs and digital ledgers. Discrepancies would be resolved within six weeks.

title: Babar says was surprised by PCB’s decision to sack Sarfraz, send seven players home
author: Dawn Sport
description: "The PCB made the decisions, so I think they would be better placed to explain them,” skipper says.
text: The Pakistan Cricket Board’s (PCB) decision to sack the national team’s head coach and send seven players back home following the defeat against England at Lord’s last week came as a surprise to captain Babar Azam, he revealed on Tuesday. The 194-run drubbing — which sealed the three-match series for the hosts — was followed by Sarfraz Ahmed’s removal as Pakistan’s head coach and Umar Gul’s dismissal as bowling coach. They were replaced by white-ball head coach Mike Hesson and Ashley Noffke, respectively. Seven players, including seasoned campaigners Imam-ul-Haq, Mohammad Rizwan and Salman Ali Agha, were axed from the squad midway through the series, while five of the replacements flown to the UK were uncapped players. The wholesale changes, as it emerged later, were planned outside the Pakistan dressing room by the national selection panel. As was the case with most members of the team’s contingent, the developments came as a surprise to Babar as well. “It was news to me as well,” Babar said during the pre-match press conference ahead of the final Test at Edgbaston. “I only found out about these things later.” Following the PCB’s dramatic move, the board’s high-performance director and selector Aaqib Javed revealed that the decision to sack the coaching staff was a reaction to their inability to make certain selection calls ahead of the second Test. While Sarfraz and Umar bore the brunt of the PCB’s action, Babar was retained to lead the side in the final Test. The captain, however, distanced himself from the board’s decisions. “But as I said, the PCB made the decisions, so I think they would be better placed to explain them,” he said. “Whatever decision the PCB has taken, as a player and as captain, I have to go along with the decision made by the cricket board. “…The PCB would have made its decision after giving it considerable thought. “In my opinion, it would be better to ask them about it because they would be able to explain it much better.” Babar also gave a straight “no” when asked whether he was aware of the PCB’s internal inquiry into the discipline and conduct of certain players. Babar and his players have little option but to put a tumultuous week behind them and focus on what they can produce on the field. To do so, however, he and Hesson have a number of fresh faces to choose from. The uncapped duo of pacer Razaullah and all-rounder Arafat Minhas could make their debuts, while Saim Ayub — who has eight Tests to his name — is likely to return to the side. Babar described the situation as an opportunity for the young players amid the chaos. “…The new players are coming in, and they have a golden opportunity to grab it and play this game,” he said, adding that the final Test, being a dead rubber, could help Pakistan handle the pressure better. “For us, this is an opportunity as a team and as a group. The series is lost, but we have nothing to lose. So we can play freely, go out onto the ground and believe in ourselves as a team,” he added. “We have had a couple of days of practice and have spoken to each other a lot. Whenever a new team or a youngster comes in, there is a little excitement, and that excitement is visible.”
