title: Reinventing widowhood
author: Our Correspondent
description: Musharraf Ali Farooqi’s novel about widowhood can also become a story of freedom and rediscovery
text: My first encounter with The Story of a Widow was in 2023. It had left me sitting with a sense of looming loneliness. Reading it this time around, that melancholy metamorphosed into an unfamiliar feeling of autonomy. The novel has drawn praise across three continents from The Edmonton Journal and The Georgia Straight in Canada to Dawn and India Today in South Asia and it is easy to see why. It is a story that manages a perfect balance of sharp social satire and a genuinely moving narrative of a woman in her fifties, learning how to want things again. Musharraf Ali Farooqi is an internationally renowned author, storyteller, educator, and award-winning translator for adults and children, and an authority on Urdu Literature. Farooqi’s novel Between Clay and Dust was a finalist for the 2012 Man Asian Prize for South Asian Prize for Literature. The Story of a Widow, shortlisted for 2011 DSC Prize for South Asian Literature. In 2018, he founded STORYKIT which develops MCI method of interactive storytelling. He is a Fellow, Harvard University South Asia Institute and has served on the advisory board of SALT Project at the University of Chicago. Since 2023, has been the Executive Director of Pakistan Spelling Bee and is currently leading the PECTAA Urdu Curriculum Reform Committee for Primary Grades. His author’s note in The Story of a Widow reveals the origin of the book. A portrait of a first husband hanging above a second husband’s chair, was encountered by the writer in someone’s living room in Toronto. This anecdote captures exactly what the novel does. It takes a small, uncanny and telling domestic image and unfolds from it an entire moral world. At its core, The Story of a Widow is a witty comedy of manners. Farooqi takes the intimate story of one woman restarting her life and expands it into something far broader: a look at family, propriety, and the invisible architecture of patriarchy that dictates life for many middle-class South Asian women. The premise is simple. Mona, after thirty-one years of marriage to Akbar Ahmad, a stern and spectacular bore of a husband, becomes a widow. Her marriage is never painted as cruel, only airless. The prologue frames widowhood itself as an inciting incident. Akbar Ahmad’s death does not end Mona’s story; rather, it opens it. In the aftermath, she finds herself in uncharted territory with seemingly absolute control over her finances, her home, and perhaps, her life. It is both funny and painfully relatable how quickly the people around Mona are certain they know what’s best for her. Into the fragile, newly found equilibrium of a woman who has just begun to rediscover herself, arrives Salamat Ali. He is an uncouth and vulgar suitor whose proposal sets off a slow-motion crisis. ‘Should a respectable widow remarry? What does she owe her daughters, her in-laws, her late husband’s memory? What, if anything, does she owe herself?’ There is no set answer to these rhetorical questions. Farooqi’s greatest achievement is refusing to let them resolve neatly. Part of what makes these questions so loaded are the double standard he lays bare through them. A remarrying widow is “looked down upon as a harlot,” while widowers are simply expected to find “virgin brides.” Mona’s caution, then, is less timidity than a rational response to a society that polices her far more than it ever polices a man. Salamat Ali is not quite a villain and nor a prize. He is exactly the kind of catalyst Mona needed, not necessarily the partner. The writer is too clever to make this novel a simple cautionary tale about a woman who could have made safer choices. The novel’s real subject is the way a woman’s body, her choices, and even her grief become communal property, argued over, managed, and moralised about by everyone except the woman herself. It’s Hina, the central character’s sister who puts this plainly, telling Mona, “You cannot have everyone else’s happiness in mind as well when you go out seeking your own. It’s not as if what you wish to do with your life is going to take away anything from theirs.” The novel’s structure traces gradual unravelling of the roles Mona has performed her whole life. She has been a dutiful wife, a defensive mother, and a respectable widow. Farooqi writes with what several reviewers have rightly called narrative clarity and restraint. There is little authorial editorialising, and the prose is spare and ironic. It is dialogue and the minutiae of domestic life such as tea trays, banarsi saris, gulab jamuns, near-missed Mughal-e-Azam cinema trip, ghazal mehfils gone wrong that are left to shoulder the emotional weight. The effect is closer comedy of manners than a melodrama, using it as a vehicle for showcasing genuine pain. One of the novel’s most captivating presences who never utters a single word is Akbar Ahmad, whose portrait is hung silently on the living-room wall and presides over the household with a persistence no living character quite matches. The portrait becomes the novel’s central symbolic device. A silent, all-seeing husband whose expression Mona reads and re-reads according to her own guilt, desire, and defiance. It is a wonderfully economical piece of craft. Farooqi doesn’t need Akbar Ahmad’s ghost to speak. Mona’s projections onto an inanimate object do all the work. Akbar Ahmad’s painted face is anything but fixed. Readers first meet him “cast in an expression of long suffering” -- the martyred countenance of a man perpetually wronged. Towards the end, that expression has turned into something far less sympathetic as he “wore a smug and vindicated look,” as though the portrait itself were keeping a score. Written with comical precision, the supporting cast reveals an author with a real ear for the cruelties and comforts of extended desi family life. It is a realistic depiction of how concern curdles into surveillance; how love and control become indistinguishable. The Story of a Widow takes family seriously as both wound and refuge. If there’s a criticism to make, it is that the novel’s plotting occasionally leans on convenient escalation rather than organic momentum. The book is also, by design, narrow in scope. It stays almost entirely within Mona’s household and immediate family, which suits it, but means readers hoping for a broader social canvas of Karachi will find the frame tightly drawn and claustrophobic. These are trivial criticisms against a novel that does exactly what it sets out to do, restore a woman’s interior life to her, in a world determined to negotiate it on her behalf. By its epilogue, Mona unspectacularly becomes someone new -- no longer performing life for anyone’s approval but her own. I often think back to my initial read, and the sorrow it awoke in me before I realised what the story had to offer. Like Mona quietly tending her garden or taking the wheel during her driving lessons, returning to this novel became an act of rediscovering myself. The Story of a Widow reminded me that a book, like a life, can mean something entirely different every time you sit with it. title: A brand new beginning
author: Omair Alavi
description: Tom Holland’s Spider-Man gets a fresh start but only after Marvel realised what made Peter Parker special
text: After years of multiverse madness, endless cameos, and an increasingly complicated Marvel Cinematic Universe, Spider-Man: Brand New Day does something surprisingly simple: it brings the focus back to Peter Parker rather than the friendly neighbourhood Spider-Man, and it works. Why? Because that’s exactly what Spider-Man needed. The fourth Tom Holland-led Spider-Man film picks up years after the events of Spider-Man: No Way Home, when Doctor Strange’s spell erased Peter Parker from everyone’s memory. His friends remember Spider-Man, but not the young man beneath the mask. Peter is therefore alone. No MJ. No Ned. No Avengers looking over his shoulder. No one knows who he really is. That loneliness becomes the foundation for a film that is considerably more personal than its title suggests. Had the title been something like ‘Spider-Man: Rediscovering Peter’ or something along those lines, it might have made more sense. Directed by Destin Daniel Cretton, Brand New Day blends street-level crime, superhero action, emotional drama, and the increasingly interconnected Marvel universe. The result is not quite the best Spider-Man film ever made — No Way Home still holds that distinction — but it may be the film that best understands what Marvel's friendly neighborhood hero needs right now. What is Spider-Man: Brand New Day about? Peter Parker (Tom Holland) has spent years protecting New York City as Spider-Man, all while living as a stranger to the people he once loved. Thanks to Doctor Strange’s spell, the world has forgotten Peter, but Peter remembers everything. MJ (Zendaya) and Ned (Jacob Batalon) have moved on with their lives, while Peter continues to fight crime and try to understand what his new life should look like. His problems become considerably more complicated when a mysterious threat begins to affect ordinary New Yorkers. Peter's investigation brings him into contact with Detective Jean DeWolff (Liza Colón-Zayas) and Bill Metzger (Tramell Tillman) of the Department of Damage Control. When he needs a friend, he turns to his Avengers family, most notably Yelena Belova, the new Black Widow (Florence Pugh), Bruce Banner, aka The Hulk (Mark Ruffalo), and Frank Castle (Jon Bernthal). As for the mysterious threat, it turns out to be a newer version of Jane Grey (Sadie Sink), who can make others do her bidding while staying in the shadows, even if it means threatening the good guys, such as Spider-Man in this case. Can Peter counter this threat, or will he fall prey to her mind tricks? Watch the film to find out. What works The biggest success of Brand New Day is the brand-new Peter Parker, who finally gets the chance to rediscover himself and his alter ego and to formulate a plan to stay alive in a city where anything can happen. Unlike the last three films, where Tom Holland plays the friendly neighbourhood Spider-Man, this time he has no superhero friend to save him. He is alone in the film, tired and heartbroken, which drives him to experiment on himself to become a better version of Spider-Man. Although he is increasingly desperate to reconnect with the people he lost, Peter doesn’t forget his duty as a superhero, which keeps his mind off many things, with MJ and Ned at the top of the list. He finally meets MJ, but not as Peter, rather as someone who lives in the neighborhood and goes by that name. She does not remember him, but he remembers everything about their relationship, creating a painful imbalance that gives their encounters genuine emotional weight. One must commend the real-life couple Tom Holland and Zendaya for their performances in such scenes, where they handle them beautifully. The film does not constantly turn their meetings into exaggerated melodrama. Instead, there is awkwardness, sadness and affection — exactly the kind of complicated emotion that makes Peter Parker work. And then there is Frank Castle, better known as The Punisher, who, as his name suggests, believes in punishing those beyond redemption, a stance that clashes with Peter’s ideology of saving lives. This unlikely relationship between Spider-Man and Punisher becomes one of the film's biggest draws, as they back each other no matter how dire the odds. Their dynamic gives Brand New Day the edge it needs to be counted among the franchise's best films. As for Sadie Sink’s Jean Grey, she is one of those characters who spends half the film as the antagonist and then becomes the hero’s supporting character as things go from bad to worse. The Stranger Things actress is a welcome addition to the Marvel Cinematic Universe and dethrones MJ as Peter’s favourite woman in the film, but only at the very end. His heart is still with MJ, who has no clue they were once together; Ned, on the other hand, is a different story altogether. The film is laced with many action sequences, some energetic, some imaginative, and, best of all, easy to follow. Spider-Man gets to show his dark side as well, even if only for a few minutes, before finally realizing the error of his ways. What makes all these fights interesting is that they carry the story forward instead of disrupting the film’s flow, and that’s why they are remembered in a good way once you exit the theater. What doesn’t work here The biggest weakness is the film's inability to fully break free from the Marvel Cinematic Universe. Every time another superhero enters the story, the film risks shifting focus from Peter to the next stage in Marvel's larger plan. Whether it’s Florence Pugh’s Black Widow or Mark Ruffalo’s Bruce Banner/The Hulk, both feel forced. They could easily have been replaced by another teacher (in Banner’s case) or a minor villain (in The Hulk’s case), whereas the information Black Widow provided could have somehow been obtained by EV, the Artificial Intelligence (voiced by Tom Holland’s first onscreen mother, Naomi Watts), which makes its MCU debut in this film. Brand New Day is at its best when it focuses on Peter Parker, and it works because it is smaller and more personal. It does not need to constantly remind audiences that Spider-Man exists within a cinematic universe with dozens of other heroes. Too much melancholy also drags the film. While many might agree it was required, for a superhero flick it was too much. You made your girlfriend forget you, man; move on! Also, Sadie Sink’s entry as Jean Grey should have been in the first 30 minutes because that would have been the beauty of it. Lingering on the suspense killed it, and by the time it was revealed, many had Googled what was happening on screen. Also, her entry scene seemed lifted from Denzel Washington's Fallen (1998), where the actor playing a detective notices a troubled soul swapping hosts to taunt him. And finally, there is plenty of Peter Parker and Spider-Man in the film, but too little of Ned, who has so far been the most trusted sidekick any Spider-Man has had across the multiverse. A little more Ned wouldn’t have hurt. Spider-Man film ranking So, is Spider-Man: Brand New Day the best Spider-Man film? Nope. One Spider-Man whose heart is broken is no match for three of them, each with their own baggage, history, and abilities. To top No Way Home, the makers of Spider-Man will have to go ballistic instead of sadistic, which is where this film went. But if the last Spidey flick had Tom Holland, Tobey Maguire and Andrew Garfield together, this one had The Punisher, Jean Grey and Spider-Man, making it a crossover event nobody expected. Instead of showing these characters battling it out, it tells the story of Peter Parker, who needs these two to save himself, return to his world, and become a better human being and an even better superhero. This film has become one of the highest-grossing films of all time because it revolves around a more grounded Peter Parker, one who has always been overshadowed by Spider-Man. The film reminds us of something Marvel occasionally seems to forget: Spider-Man is interesting because Peter Parker is interesting. If you go back to Spider-Man’s origins, you will realise that this Peter Parker is closest to the one Stan Lee created sixty years ago. He was meant to be broke, living with his aunt, struggling for money, holding onto the only job he could get, and facing the same issues any young person would in downtown New York. Tom Holland plays that young man well, portraying someone who is trying to do the right thing while dealing with loneliness, responsibility, money, relationships, and the consequences of his own choices. It may not be the best Spider-Man movie ever made, but after years of increasingly complex superhero storytelling, it could be the film that gives Marvel what it desperately needed: a brand-new beginning. title: PSG go for three in a row as UCL returns
author: AFP
description: The French giants encounter a testing schedule
text: Another UEFA Champions League season gets going this week with the beginning of the league phase as Paris Saint-Germain bid to join the tiny band of clubs to have won the competition three years running. PSG successfully defended their title last season when they beat Arsenal on penalties in Budapest, retaining the trophy they won for the first time in their history 12 months earlier. Luis Enrique's side have already secured their status as one of the competition's greatest teams by winning it back-to-back, something only Real Madrid had previously achieved since the inception of the modern Champions League in 1992. Winning three in a row would be on another level entirely. Real did exactly that under Zinedine Zidane between 2016 and 2018, The only other teams to manage such a feat are Ajax (1971-73) and Bayern Munich (1974-76), while Madrid also won the first five editions of the European Cup from 1956 to 1960. "Our objectives are clear. I want to win important trophies and there are none more important than the Champions League," said Luis Enrique, who also led Barcelona to glory in 2015. The back-to-back titles for the French giants have coincided with the introduction of the new Champions League format, with 36 teams in the league phase now playing eight games against eight different opponents. The Parisians struggled in the league phase in each of the last two campaigns, finishing outside the top eight and having to come through the additional play-off round to make the last 16. Tough draws were partly responsible for that, and PSG will face some familiar opponents this time in Manchester City, Barcelona and Aston Villa. With each passing year, the prospect of a team other than one of Europe's super clubs winning the Champions League seems more remote. Arsenal to take next step? The Premier League's financial strength means all of its representatives can be expected to feature prominently, with Arsenal chief among them. Over the last three years, the Gunners have lost in the quarter-finals, the semi-finals, and then the final. There is therefore a logical next step for Mikel Arteta's side, Arsenal topped the league phase last season with a perfect record. They have a tough start this time away to Napoli. There are five English clubs involved, with Manchester City and Liverpool joined by the returning Manchester United and Villa. Bayern Munich are formidable, while Jose Mourinho has returned to Real Madrid charged with the task of leading them back to continental glory. Barcelona are itching to get their hands on the trophy again. It is hard to see beyond one of those clubs, although Inter Milan could have a say and Atletico Madrid will be desperate to reach a final to be held in their stadium. Debutants The only club outside Spain, England, Germany, Italy and France to have won the Champions League in the last 30 years remains Mourinho's Porto in 2004. Plenty of new names will add freshness to the competition, including Como, who finished fourth in Serie A last season under Cesc Fabregas to qualify at the expense of AC Milan and Juventus. Viking Stavanger are in the Champions League proper for the first time after winning a first Norwegian title in 34 years. Sabah start with a trip to Old Trafford after winning a first Azerbaijani title and coming through four qualifying ties. Their manager, Valdas Dambrauskas, got into coaching with the money he made appearing on the Lithuanian version of 'Who Wants to be a Millionaire'. "Since I was 12, when I realised I will not be a professional player, I knew I wanted to be a football coach," he said in an interview with Flashscore. "I cannot guess what would have happened without this game, but I believe I would have found a way to achieve my dream." Sabah might not qualify for the next stage -- although compatriots Qarabag did that last season -- but just being in the league phase is worth almost 20 million euros ($23.2m) at a minimum, significant sums for clubs from lesser leagues. The Champions League winners pocket around 90 million euros in prize money, before adding millions more, notably from television -- it is understood PSG earned around 150 million euros for each of their last two victories.

title: The pot-luck makes a comeback
author: Fouzia Nasir Ahmad
description: It’s not nostalgia, but necessity -- why busy lives and unreliable utilities are bringing shared meals back
text: There was a time when inviting a dozen people to dinner was less a social occasion than a military operation. The truly accomplished hostess knew the art of dawat. Her biryani emerged from the kitchen with every grain separate, her keema-filled aloo cutlets were uniformly shaped and perfectly golden, the raita was chilled, the salad artistically arranged and the dessert made from scratch. Fresh flowers appeared in vases. The prized china was brought out. The dining table looked as if it had been waiting all week to get on Instagram and create a buzz in the circles. She knew exactly how much rice 14 people would eat, how many kebabs could disappear before the main course and, presumably, the precise number of minutes required to make everything look effortless. The rest of us, awed, merely watched in admiration. Today, however, the Pakistani dawat is confronting a less glamorous question: How exactly do you host 12 people when you don't know whether you will have water, gas or electricity? The answer, increasingly, seems to be: don't just show up. Bring a dish. The potluck — once associated with casual gatherings, student parties and perhaps a slightly Western idea of communal eating — appears to be finding its way back into our social lives. But this time, it is not necessarily because we have suddenly become adventurous about sharing our culinary skills. It is because life has become too unpredictable, too expensive and too exhausting to put an entire dawat on one person's shoulders. “I would like to make lasagna or a coconut chicken curry or karhai but I’m at work and commuting back at day end, while the gas supply starts at 6.30 pm,” says Shaheen. “By the time I reach it is already 7.30pm and there is not enough energy or time to cook. Plus gas supply becomes almost nothing when people start using pressure pumps. So it is easier for me to take ice cream or mithai.” “I have a cook who comes in for two hours and cooks food for a week for us, meeting our dietary requirements,” says Laila. “And in the time slot that we have with gas supply, we only get him to cook that. So if there is a potluck, for instance, then I order something from outside to take with me.” In these circumstances, the host can prepare a lemon-mint cooler to welcome guests and perhaps serve an appetiser. The main course and dessert arrive with the guests. It sounds simple. And perhaps that is exactly why it works. Consider the logistics of the old-fashioned dawat. If there is water, there may be no gas. If there is gas, the electricity may disappear. A generator may be roaring in the background while guests sit around the dining table by candlelight instead of soft music. And if you have no water stored, the prospect of washing a dozen plates, glasses, serving dishes and pieces of treasured china can be enough to cancel the dinner altogether. Paper plates and disposable containers are fast replacing dinnerware at get-togethers. “How will we wash it all? Tankers supplying water are so expensive?” says Fareeha. “Having guests over also means water being used in the toilets and there is a chance of going over our week’s water supply. For people like me, who love to entertain at home, these things are worrying and annoying. I’m quite embarrassed to have people over to my house in this way but what to do?” Her question captures something larger than a reluctance to dirty good crockery. The infrastructure of hospitality has changed. So has the price. Taking a large group to a restaurant can cost a small fortune, while the experience is not necessarily worth the bill. At home, meanwhile, the cost of meat, rice, cooking oil, vegetables and dessert has made the traditional dawat an increasingly expensive exercise. Add the cost of a water tanker, generator fuel or an emergency cylinder of gas and entertaining guests begins to look less like hospitality and more like project management. Yet the desire to gather has not disappeared. And perhaps that is because we come from cultures where food has never simply been food. Across the subcontinent, feeding people is an expression of affection, generosity, family and belonging. A guest is not merely offered food; a guest is urged to eat more. Thora sa aur lijiye is almost a cultural reflex. The first refusal is politely ignored, the second is negotiated and the third may be taken as a personal insult. Our celebrations, family visits and social occasions have traditionally revolved around food. The table is expected to look abundant. There must be enough for everyone, and then some. The traditional dawat grew out of this culture of generosity but, over time, hospitality also became a performance — particularly for women. The hostess was expected not simply to feed people but to demonstrate that she could feed them beautifully. There was an entire choreography to it: the spotless house, the tablecloth, the flowers, the serving dishes, platters of hot food arriving at precisely the right moment. And then came the ritual denial: Aray, kuch bhi nahin banaya! Nothing at all. Just biryani, two curries, kebabs, cutlets, salad, raita and three desserts. The truly accomplished hostess could make abundance look effortless. But perhaps that is the part of our hospitality that is becoming difficult to sustain. There is also the small matter of time. Most people are clocked in, commuting through increasingly congested cities, rushing from work to home and from one obligation to another. Children have school, tuition, workouts, walks, sports and endless activities. There are elderly parents, household errands, bills, emails and WhatsApp messages. Even when people are technically off work, they are not necessarily free. The leisurely afternoon spent chopping, marinating, cooking, laying the table and arranging flowers before guests arrive belongs increasingly to another era. Someone leaving work at six may not reach home until seven or later. By then, the ambition of making that elaborate coconut chicken curry has disappeared somewhere between the office and the traffic jam. So she brings ice cream. Or mithai. And why shouldn't she? The point of attending a dinner is not to prove that she can cook. This may be the most interesting thing about the return of the potluck. It is not necessarily introducing a new culture of communal eating to South Asia. It may actually be returning us to something we already had — the idea that feeding people is a shared act. What changed was that communal hospitality gradually became the responsibility of one household, and often one woman. The potluck distributes that responsibility again. One person brings biryani. Another brings kebabs. Someone orders a curry. Another arrives with dessert. Someone else brings salad, raita, mithai or drinks. The contribution does not even have to be homemade. The host provides the space and, perhaps, one or two things. Most importantly, the host provides the gathering. This is not a competition in culinary experimentation. Nobody expects the guest assigned dessert to arrive with a deconstructed pistachio soufflé. It is simply a practical way of saying: I want to be there, and this is what I can bring. That is rather different from the old model of hospitality, where the hostess had to make everything possible. And perhaps there is something liberating about it. For generations, Pakistani women in particular have been expected to demonstrate love through food. Feeding people generously was proof of good upbringing, good housekeeping and sometimes even good marriage. A successful hostess did not merely serve dinner; she demonstrated competence. Otherwise, what will people say, would be the over-riding thought! The potluck quietly removes some of that pressure. Nobody has to spend the day in the kitchen. Nobody has to produce restaurant-quality food for 15 people. Nobody has to worry about whether the china matches the flowers. Nobody has to apologise because the electricity went out halfway through cooking. And nobody has to pretend that it was all effortless. There is something democratic about everyone arriving with one dish. The labour is shared. The expense is shared. The risk is shared. Even the failures can be shared. Perhaps that is why the potluck feels less like a decline in hospitality than an adaptation of it. We still want to gather. We still want to feed one another. We still want to sit around a table and talk long after the food has been cleared. We still want the laughter, the gossip, the family stories and the inevitable argument about who makes the best biryani. What we no longer have, reliably, is the infrastructure — or perhaps the money, time and energy — to stage the grand dawat that once made such gatherings possible. The potluck may therefore be less a Western import than a modern solution to an old South Asian instinct. We have not stopped wanting to feed one another. We have simply stopped pretending that one person can do it all. So bring the biryani. Bring the cutlets. Bring the dessert. And please don't bring the china. Nobody knows when the water is coming back.

title: Old iron, new drugs: The fight for natural muscle
author: Riaz Ahmed
description: A 64-year-old coach remains a staunch advocate of old-school training in an age of shortcuts
text: Inside the weight room of the Peshawar Sports Complex, the rhythmic clinking of iron plates reverberates against concrete walls long before the rest of the city awakens. Plates are loaded onto steel bars, mirrors reflect young athletes lifting and pushing weights, and iron hits the floor with thunderous clang. Heavy breathing of the men exercising punctuates the noise of the machinery. Observing every move of the trainers in the gym is 64-year-old Shiraz Muhammad. He tracks their reps. His catches details that less experienced eyes miss: an elbow flaring out too far during a bench press, a heel lifting slightly off the wooden platform during a heavy squat, or a shoulder rounding under stress. With a quick gesture or a firm word, he steps in to adjust the men’s form. A lifelong resident of Mohalla Shah Wali Qatal, nestled within the densely packed lanes of the historic old Qissa Khwani area inside Peshawar’s ancient walled city, Shiraz carries the nostalgia of a bygone era. He serves as a veteran coach overseeing bodybuilding, weightlifting, and powerlifting at the sports complex. But to the generations of lifters who pass through these doors, he represents far more than an instructor. He is a living bridge linking Pakistan’s golden age of natural athletic training with today’s fast-paced, modern gym culture. The fitness landscape has shifted dramatically since he began his training in 1982. At that time Arnold Schwarzenegger was a global icon and growth hormones were not discussed. Fitness and weight lifting were niche hobbies – or rather a passion – for they were only for the few who could commit to live a clean and healthy lifestyle after spending hours at the gym to chisel their bodies. Over the decades, fitness in Pakistan bloomed into an industry and the original bodybuilders, who trained in the traditional natural discipline, saw the dramatic advancement toward commercialisation and instant physical transformations. The industry increasingly normalised synthetic enhancements, anabolic steroids, and growth hormones among young gym-goers. The gym facilities when he started training at Qayyum Stadium – part of the Peshawar Sports Complex – during the early 1980s bore little resemblance to today’s air-conditioned commercial fitness clubs. It was essentially an open-air ground equipped with raw, heavy free weights, cast-iron discs, homemade barbells, and sturdy wooden benches. There were no cable pulleys, no padded leg extension machines, and no heart-rate monitors. The training environment was bare, exposed to the elements, and reliant entirely on the grit of the men who gathered there. Knowledge was limited, but enthusiasm was high. What the young men learned about fitness came from word-of-mouth. Shiraz mentioned his first teacher was Sohail Durrani. “There was no internet then. Our only source of information was bodybuilding magazines,” he said. He and other trainees would visit London Book Depot to buy magazines, sometimes second-hand, for Rs50 each. “They had workout tips for young bodybuilders and we followed them in the absence of proper coaches.” Steroids, growth hormones and even protein powders were unknown in Pakistan then. Diets consisted mainly of eggs and chicken. “Our tools were basic and simple, but our approach was modern. We knew there was no shortcut in bodybuilding.” During this golden era of international bodybuilding, Schwarzenegger was global pop culture's ultimate muscle icon, celebrated worldwide for his massive frame and cinematic presence. But while many young Pakistani athletes sought to copy Arnold’s sheer mass, Shiraz found his true aesthetic inspiration in a different legend of the era: Frank Zane. Known in the bodybuilding world as "The Chemist" for his meticulous approach to physical sculpture, Frank Zane championed a physique built around razor-sharp conditioning, narrow waistlines, wide shoulders, perfect symmetry, and classic proportion rather than overwhelming bulk. Dr Sahibzada Mehmood Noor, dean and chief executive officer of the Lady Reading Hospital in Peshawar, has been a student of Coach Shiraz for the past two decades. “There are very well equipped and modern gyms out there but I still go to a government gym at Peshawar Sports Complex because I do not value gym equipment. I focus mainly on the quality of coaching and proper techniques,” Dr Noor said while talking to The Express Tribune. About the widespread use of drugs by bodybuilders, he said that most people use testosterone hormones for muscle mass. “Our body normally controls production of testosterones. When we take testosterone in large quantities, it disturbs the natural body mechanism. It impacts the natural production of sperm resulting in infertility,” he added. “The long-term use of testosterone can result in diabetes and even death as well,” he said. “Testosterone is a male sex hormone which naturally makes muscles, sperm and is responsible for all of our manly features in the body. On the other hand, anabolic steroids are manufactured and their overdose could be fatal,” he added. “When you exercise, it naturally increases your muscle mass and subsequently results in increased testosterone production. Exercise burns calories. The more you burn calories, the muscular you become,” he said. In recent decades, performance enhancement drugs and steroids have developed into an underground black economy. There are anabolic steroids mostly made from testosterone and in the medical world it is used under the strict supervision of an endocrinologist because of their serious side effects. When non-professional people, like a bodybuilding coach, give it to their trainees, it will result in serious side effects and medical complications, he explained. Today’s young lifters are constantly bombarded with curated images of hyper-muscular physiques on smartphone screens. This constant visual pressure, combined with a cultural desire for fast results, has created an environment where patience is increasingly rare. In many commercial gyms across urban centres, the traditional emphasis on long-term skill acquisition, progressive overload, and organic muscle building has been replaced by a search for chemical shortcuts. Anabolic steroids, growth hormones, veterinary compounds, and unverified chemical stacks are now easily accessible to young gym-goers. Eager to pack on massive amounts of muscle mass in a matter of months rather than years, many novitiates jump straight to dangerous pharmaceutical cycles before they have even mastered basic squat or deadlift technique. When asked about the use of supplements which some people confuse with steroids and performance drugs, Dr Noor said that supplements are totally different from steroids. “Multivitamins and protein powders are supplements. They are not harmful if you have vitamin deficiency or you want to boost your protein intake,” Dr Noor said, adding that supplements are not performance enhancing drugs and don’t have side effects. “But we have to be very careful because some manufacturers mix steroids with proteins or other medicines and supplements to make their product more attractive for the end users. So I would recommend going for a reputed brand when using them,” he added. The nutritional culture In the 1980s, the modern multi-billion-dollar sports supplement industry had not yet arrived in Pakistan. Commercial protein powders, pre-workout formulas, branched-chain amino acids, and creatine were entirely nonexistent in local markets. Furthermore, performance-enhancing substances like anabolic steroids and human growth hormones were virtually unknown among regional lifters. Physiques were constructed purely through real food, rest, and hard labour. A bodybuilder’s diet in Karachi or Peshawar was straightforward, unrefined, and rooted in wholesome local foods. Protein came directly from farm-fresh eggs, whole chicken, fresh milk, lentils, and meat-based traditional dishes prepared at home. Carbohydrates were provided by whole wheat rotis, rice, and seasonal fruits. Physical growth was slow, steady, and incremental—built stone by stone over years of consistent natural effort and natural recovery. “Our 1980s generation of bodybuilders is unique in many ways. Firstly, we were all natural as far as the diet plan is concerned. Secondly, we used free weights which were difficult to master but very effective in building muscles,” Shiraz explained, adding that after entering the gym, he used to do 500 bodyweight squats followed by weighted squats as a trainee. “Without a proper protein-rich diet, technique and a comprehensive workout plan there will be no progress. A coach will tell you about your workout as well as diet,” he said. At the peak of his training, Shiraz ate 40 eggs and a whole chicken daily and hit the gym three times a day. “We worked two muscle groups in the morning and evening. The noon session was for cardio, which many bodybuilders now consider taboo.” He stresses that a solid physique requires five years of consistent work. “Today players want results in six months using steroids and growth hormones, which often lead to premature deaths and heart problems. My generation of bodybuilders is still healthy.” With few coaches available in Peshawar for diet and advanced techniques in the 1980s, he travelled to Lahore once a month to train under Muhammad Azam Bajwa, a former Mr Asia. From 1985 to 1996 his diet was strict: eggs, salad and chicken across five meals a day, with no carbohydrates, milk, yoghurt or bread. The only occasional cheat meal was custard at weddings. His weight has remained steady at 75 kg from the day he started bodybuilding through his national championship years to date. Online videos and social media hype Beyond the rise of performance-enhancing drugs, another dangerous trend has emerged in recent years: young lifters substituting structured, long-term training under a qualified mentor with online video tutorials and social media hype. Over the past two decades, the explosion of social media platforms, digital video channels, and modern commercial fitness centers across Pakistan has transformed traditional bodybuilding into a fast-moving, image-obsessed industry. Today’s gym-goers are constantly bombarded with online content promising rapid, effortless transformations. “Most people avoid a professional coach these days. Instead, they go for online videos and tutorials which promise a great body within no time,” Shiraz explains. He points out that watching short clips—such as plank exercises or routine breakdown videos—on a mobile screen and attempting to copy them blindly in the gym offers no practical benefit. “These YouTubers have created an overhype in order to attract as many views as possible to make money,” Shiraz says, stressing that exercise is only one component of a much larger equation. “A coach will tell you about your workout as well as your diet. Proper technique is also very important. Without a proper protein-rich diet, technique, and a comprehensive workout plan, there will be no progress.” Training without the direct supervision of a veteran coach not only stalls muscle growth but significantly increases the risk of severe injuries, which often causes discouraged beginners to quit the sport altogether. “Over the years, I have noted that by copying YouTube you can increase your stamina despite the risk of severe injuries, but you cannot make a good body because no one is there to correct your mistakes,” Shiraz said. “You need proper angles and proper technique to see growth in your body. As a coach and teacher, I see that only 10 out of 100 people can use a dumbbell properly for a shoulder workout. This is because of YouTube videos, and if your technique is incorrect, you are inviting injuries.” “By copying YouTube videos, you can increase your stamina despite the risk of severe injuries but you cannot make a good body because no one is there to correct your mistakes,” he argued. Dr Noor also urges the new generation to return to foundational, natural methods. He advises: “As a doctor, I would suggest that youngsters should not opt for shortcuts and they should go for natural bodybuilding, which is time-consuming but long-lasting.” In his long coaching career, Shiraz estimates he has trained more than 10,000 women and over 30,000 men. Currently he serves as an official judge of the Bodybuilding Association, vice-president of the Pakistan Weightlifting Federation and president of the Khyber-Pakhtunkhwa Weightlifting Association. “No one comes to me to learn bodybuilding the old way anymore,” he said, adding that in recent decades he himself mastered the art of using gym machines but still natural bodybuilding techniques advocated and taught by him are seen to be too slow by many people. “Now the concept of using free weights only is almost gone. There are machines which are easy to use. This has changed the technique altogether,” he said. “The most unfortunate thing is that the natural, original Arnold-style approach has been lost. I advise parents to watch their children,” Shiraz warned. “If they see a major physical change within three months of joining a gym, they should ask questions. A natural body takes three to five years to develop, not three to six months.”

title: Boxing fades, four fight on
author: Alam Zeb Safi
description: Pakistan sends two men, two women to Japan Asian Games as funding, exposure remain hurdles
text: Once regarded as one of Pakistan’s strongest prospects for medals at the Asian Games, boxing heads into this month’s continental showpiece with modest expectations and a four-member squad. Pakistan has not won an Asian Games boxing medal since the 2014 Incheon Games, when Mohammad Waseem secured bronze. Waseem has since moved into the professional boxing and has become a WBA World Gold champion. The drought continued at the 2018 Asian Games in Jakarta and the 2023 Games in Hangzhou, with Pakistan’s boxers failing to reach the podium. This time, the country will field two men and two women at the Games in Japan, which formally open on September 19. Sumama Rahman will compete in the 55kg category, while Irfan Khan will enter the 92kg division. Fatima Zehra will fight at 60kg and Maria Rind at 51kg. The squad has been training at the Pakistan Sports Complex in Islamabad since August 24 after the Pakistan Boxing Federation (PBF) conducted an earlier camp in Rawalpindi with the assistance from the army and the Pakistan Olympic Association (POA). “Yes, the army backed us, more especially administratively, and we are thankful to them,” PBF president Col Nasir Tung told The Express Tribune. Tariq Siddiqui of WAPDA and Liaquat Mughal of Navy will accompany the boxers to Japan. The financial constraints surrounding the team underline one of the sport's biggest problems in Pakistan, the limited resources for international competition. Pakistan Sports Board (PSB) will sponsor one male and one female boxer, while the federation will cover the remaining members of the delegation. “Yes, what we can as Board sponsors only two boxers,” Nasir said. For the federation, the challenge goes beyond funding a single Asian Games campaign. Nasir said Pakistan’s boxers lacked the international exposure needed to build rankings and gain experience against stronger oppositions. “We don’t have corporate sector support and state also does not back us that much and it’s not easy to ensure maximum participation of boxers in international circuit,” he said. That lack of competition has a direct impact on Pakistan’s prospects at major events, he added. “Unless you give exposure to boxers they will not improve,” Nasir said. The Asian Games draw will be particularly demanding, with established boxing nations from Central Asia joined by strong contenders from countries including Iran, India, Thailand and hosts Japan. “It’s not easy to win medal in this belt,” Nasir said. Despite the difficult road, he identified Fatima Zehra as Pakistan’s chance of making a deep run. “Yes, she is capable of reaching the podium provided she gets good draws,” he said, while pointing again to the problem of rankings caused by limited international exposure. Zehra’s prospects are supported by her recent performance at the Commonwealth Games, where she won bronze after an extended development programme backed by the federation. Nasir said the result demonstrated what greater preparation and exposure could produce. “You know we groomed Fatima Zehra too much and the result was also inspiring as she won bronze in the Commonwealth Games,” he said. The federation’s financial limitations have also affected the selection and participation of other promising fighters. Maria Rind, who comes from Karachi’s Lyari area, was included in Pakistan’s Commonwealth Games squad but ultimately could not travel because of a lack of resources. Rind has competed at a handful of international events during her career and will now have another opportunity to test herself on the Asian stage. For Irfan Khan, the tournament will mark a bigger milestone. The fighter from Khyber Pakhtunkhwa is set to make his international debut, stepping into one of the sport’s toughest competitive regions without the benefit of extensive international experience. Sumama Rahman and Fatima Zehra, meanwhile, already have experience and will be looking to build on it in Japan. The team is due to leave for Japan on September 17, two days before the opening ceremony.

title: PSX comes under selling pressure, sheds 1,003.40 points by midday
author: Our Correspondent
description: Oil surge amid Hormuz tensions weighs on OMCs, banks, autos, cement and refineries
text: The Pakistan Stock Exchange (PSX) came under renewed selling pressure on Monday, with the benchmark KSE-100 index losing 1,003.40 points or 0.57% to 174,325.42 by 1:29 pm midday, as rising oil prices and heightened geopolitical tensions over the Strait of Hormuz weighed on investor sentiment. The index opened the week on a fragile note, falling 429.59 points, or 0.25%, to 174,899.23 at 9.39am in early trading. It later oscillated between an intraday high of 175,353.67 and a low of 174,313.12. Selling pressure was witnessed across key sectors, including oil marketing companies (OMCs), automobile assemblers, cement, commercial banks and refineries. Market activity remained active, with around 100.91 million shares changing hands by midday. The traded value stood at approximately Rs5.87 billion. The previous close of the KSE-100 stood at 175,328.82. The pressure in the local market came against a backdrop of rising international oil prices. Oil prices rose by more than $1 a barrel on Monday as tit-for-tat strikes between the United States and Iran involving vessels sailing through the Strait of Hormuz and other areas heightened concerns over a prolonged disruption to Middle Eastern oil supplies. Read: Geopolitical tensions drag stocks down Iran also said it would announce a new restricted zone in the Gulf in the coming days, along with maps for a new shipping corridor through the Strait of Hormuz. The announcement followed a weekend exchange of strikes involving shipping, further raising concerns in global energy markets. Higher oil prices are particularly important for Pakistan's equity market given their potential implications for the country's import bill, inflation and external financing requirements, while also raising concerns over corporate margins in oil-sensitive sectors. The KSE-100's decline therefore reflected a combination of geopolitical uncertainty, higher global oil prices and broad-based profit-taking, with investors remaining cautious amid heightened external risks.

title: The power of play
author: Tufail Ahmed
description: Why games and human connection are the real key to lifelong mental sharpness
text: Since its meteoric rise into a global digital phenomenon, solving the daily Wordle has become a ritual for millions of people. Every morning alongside a cup of coffee or during commute hours, people log on to solve a grid of six rows and five letters to guess the word of the day. Players proudly share their daily scores, analyse strategic opening words, and celebrate brief moments of victory over a six-try limit. But beyond the satisfaction of maintaining a streak, the viral popularity of games like Wordle raises a fundamental question: Are these daily digital word puzzles genuinely boosting our brain power, or are they simply a delightful distraction? This modern fascination with quick, daily puzzles is not a brand-new phenomenon– rather, it is the digital evolution of a habit adults have relied on for generations to wind down. While Wordle serves as a quick morning spark to wake up the brain, many people instinctively reach for similar language puzzles at the close of the day to achieve the exact opposite effect. Consider the common habit of winding down in the evening, when the day’s work is done, with a paper crossword. For millions of people around the world, sitting in bed with a newsprint puzzle and a pencil has long been a comforting evening ritual—a bridge between the frantic pace of the workday and the stillness of sleep. Instead of doomscrolling through bright smartphone screens that keep the mind wired, filling in a few clues provides a structured, quiet focus. It absorbs intrusive thoughts, helping the active mind transition out of work mode and signalling that it is finally time to release stress. A late-night crossword on a nightstand, a weekly carrom tournament in the courtyard, or an evening match of Ludo with extended family—scenes like these were once a natural part of daily life across Pakistan. Today, however, as work culture expands to consume every waking hour and screen time dominates our leisure, play has increasingly been relegated to childhood. Adult life is governed by a rigid metric of productivity, where time spent outside work, family care, or domestic duties is often viewed with subtle guilt. Yet, far from being a frivolous pastime or merely a sleep aid, an emerging body of public health research suggests that engaging in mentally stimulating, socially interactive games is a foundational pillar of long-term cognitive resilience. As life expectancies rise, preserving mental sharpness into our later years has become a priority. Many turn to digital apps, word puzzles, or complex board games in hopes of resisting cognitive decline. But what actually happens inside the brain when we sit down to play, and how can a simple game help us live healthier lives? The limits of digital "brain training" In recent years, a multibillion-dollar industry has emerged around commercial "brain-training" applications. Marketed as high-tech solutions to safeguard the aging brain, these digital games promise to enhance memory, boost focus, and even keep neurodegenerative conditions like Alzheimer’s disease at bay. A 2015 survey revealed that 40 percent of older Americans actively engaged in puzzles specifically for brain health—ranking mental games ahead of sleep, exercise, and diet as their preferred habit for staying sharp. However, scientific evidence surrounding the effectiveness of computerised brain games remains mixed. One major review noted that while specialised games make players better at the specific tasks within the software, there is little evidence these skills transfer to everyday real-world cognitive abilities. The consensus among health experts is clear: brain games cannot reverse dementia, and many commercial claims made by brain-training companies are exaggerated. “Games can engage several cognitive functions at the same time, including attention, working memory, planning, decision-making, mental flexibility, language, visuospatial skills and problem-solving,” said Muhammad Hamza Atiq, who teaches at the psychiatry department of AKUH. “For example, chess requires planning, working memory and anticipating an opponent's moves; bridge involves memory, probability, attention and social communication; crosswords and word games involve language and retrieval; while many board games require decision-making, mental flexibility and adapting to changing circumstances,” he told The Express Tribune. This broad spectrum of mental mechanics explains why variety is key. Relying solely on a single daily Wordle or late-night crossword creates a narrow proficiency, whereas engaging with different types of mental challenges yields a well-rounded cognitive exercise. “There is evidence that intellectually stimulating leisure activities can improve aspects of cognitive functioning, particularly when they involve learning new skills, communication and sustained mental engagement,” Atiq said. “However, we should not claim that one particular type of game is universally superior. Different games exercise different cognitive abilities, and the evidence suggests that variety may be useful. A game is more likely to stimulate the brain when a person has to think, make decisions, remember information, learn strategies and adapt to new situations.” Learning new skills To understand why play is so vital, one must look at how the brain adapts to novel challenges over time. According to recommendations from the Global Council on Brain Health (GCBH), engaging in lifelong mentally challenging activities builds cognitive resilience over time. Whether it is playing a high-stakes match of bridge or carom, structured play deploys four distinct neurological mechanisms. Firstly, they establish sustained attention. Games force the mind out of passive consumption and require active concentration on rules, clues, spatial changes, and live variables. Secondly, they activate your memory. Players must constantly recall past moves, hidden cards, active constraints, or vocabulary strategies. Thirdly, playing games employs brain functions to make strategic choices. They demand decision-making, impulse control, and rapid adaptation when circumstances change. Lastly, physical sports and active outdoor games add a metabolic layer, increasing cardiovascular fitness and benefiting overall cognitive health. “There is encouraging evidence that cognitive and recreational activities can help maintain aspects of cognitive function as we age,” said Atiq. “Systematic reviews of tabletop and board games have found improvements in global cognition and executive functioning, particularly among older adults.” Yet, he points out that looking at long-term outcomes requires more precision. “We need to be careful about saying that playing games prevents Alzheimer's disease or dementia,” Atiq said. “The evidence is much stronger for improving or maintaining certain cognitive abilities than it is for proving that games prevent dementia. For example, a large longitudinal study found that people who regularly played board games had a lower risk of dementia, but importantly, this association became much weaker after accounting for baseline cognition and depression. This illustrates why observational studies cannot establish that the game itself caused the lower dementia risk. So my interpretation would be: Games are a promising component of healthy cognitive aging, but they should not be marketed as a way of preventing dementia.” The World Health Organisation’s 2026 recommendations reflect this view, specifically incorporating cognitive stimulation and social engagement as key elements in a broader strategy to reduce cognitive decline risk. The science of human connection While solo digital puzzles provide a peaceful, low-pressure way to engage the mind, multiplayer games—like bridge, carrom, chess, or board games—offer a crucial dimension that screens and solo exercises lack – human interaction. Social connection is not merely a pleasant byproduct of playing together; it is an intensive neurological exercise in its own right. A live interaction requires reading micro-expressions, interpreting subtle intentions, anticipating verbal responses, regulating emotional reactions, and maintaining active conversation. “This may be one of the most important aspects of playing games,” explained Atiq. “Social interaction itself requires considerable brain activity. We have to listen, remember what another person has said, interpret intentions, anticipate responses, regulate our emotions and adapt our behavior. Therefore, a social game may provide several forms of mental stimulation simultaneously.” A game such as chess or bridge is not simply a cognitive exercise, he said. When played with other people, it combines cognitive stimulation with social interaction, communication, emotional engagement and a sense of belonging. There is also increasing evidence that social isolation and poor social relationships are associated with cognitive decline in older adults. “Conversely, social participation appears to be protective, although the precise causal relationship is complex. Randomised studies of social-interaction interventions suggest that social engagement can have beneficial effects particularly on executive functioning, although the evidence is not strong enough to say that social interaction alone prevents dementia,” he explained further. For many adults, particularly older individuals navigating empty nests or retirement, the emotional and social nourishment provided by a weekly gathering unmatched. “So I would say that the companionship may be almost as important as the game itself for some people,” Atiq observes. “A weekly bridge or chess group provides cognitive stimulation, social contact, routine, enjoyment and a reason to leave the house and interact with others.” Disease prevention Given the widespread fear surrounding neurodegenerative diseases, it is understandable why people eagerly grab onto any habit that promises absolute protection. But health professionals warn against treating play as a singular medical prescription. “There is no particular board game, card game or brain-training program that has been proven to prevent Alzheimer's disease, depression, stroke or cancer by itself. Rather, games can be one component of a lifestyle that reduces risk,” clarified Atiq. Similarly, physical activity reduces the risk of cardiovascular disease, hypertension, stroke, type 2 diabetes and several cancers, and is associated with better mental health and cognitive health. “So rather than saying playing games prevents dementia, I would say games are one enjoyable way of incorporating these activities into everyday life, in order to maintain one’s intellectual abilities. Reclaiming leisure time In a society that equates value strictly with output, making room for play requires a conscious shift in mindset. Across Pakistani culture, leisure is frequently treated as an afterthought or a luxury reserved for those who have exhausted every other responsibility. “I think we need to change our perception of play,” emphasised Atiq. “In many societies, including ours, playing games is sometimes viewed as something children do and adults should have outgrown. Adults are expected to work, study, earn money and fulfil family responsibilities, while leisure is sometimes regarded as unproductive. We should recognise that healthy leisure is not wasted time.” The best incentive is that reclaiming play does not demand costly subscriptions or high-tech gear. The most impactful habits are often low-cost and easily integrated into daily routines. “I would encourage families to deliberately make time for play,” suggests Atiq. “It doesn't have to mean spending hours on a game. It could be a family board game once or twice a week; a game of chess or cards with friends; a crossword or word puzzle; badminton or table tennis; walking or playing a sport with friends; learning a new game or skill; and community-based games for older adults.” The emphasis should be on regularity, enjoyment and social connection rather than competition or performance. “Most importantly,” concluded Atiq, “playing should complement and not replace the fundamentals of brain health which are physical activity, adequate sleep, healthy diet, social relationships, control of hypertension and diabetes, avoidance of tobacco and harmful alcohol use, and treatment of depression and other medical conditions.” In our pursuit of healthy living, we often forget that well-being is not just about avoiding illness—it is about nurturing joy, curiosity, and connection. Setting aside time each day to play, whether over a grid on a screen, a board with family, or a pencil and paper puzzle before bed, may just be one of the simplest, most rewarding investments in our long-term health.

title: Is Nepal a turning point in climate coverage?
author: Mark Hertsgaard
description: More news outlets need to connect the latest disaster to global warming
text: It’s been slow coming, but news coverage of climate change may at last be turning a corner. For years, reporting on climate-related disasters — the super-storm Hurricane Helene that blasted the southeastern US in 2024, the mega-fires that torched Los Angeles in 2025, the record heat that has scorched Europe and Asia in 2026 — rarely mentioned the words “climate change,” despite overwhelming scientific evidence linking such extreme events to human-caused global heating. This week, however, even formerly reticent news outlets are making the climate connection clear in their coverage of the deadly flooding in Nepal, where more than 1,100 are confirmed dead and an additional 4,000 are missing. More such disasters are sure to follow. Even with unprecedented emissions reductions, global temperatures will rise to at least 1.8 degrees Celsius above pre-Industrial levels, the UN Environment Programme announced last week. As rising temperatures melt more glacial ice, “we can expect more and more of these events, a greater frequency, a greater magnitude,” Alton C. Byers of the University of Colorado, Boulder, said at a Covering Climate Now live conversation on the Nepal floods. Meanwhile, The Guardian, Agence France-Presse, The New York Times, the Associated Press, Bloomberg, Deutsche Welle, and other outlets whose reporting has long reflected established climate science, suddenly, are no longer outliers. The shift is particularly striking among US television networks, whose climate coverage had declined by 35% during the first year of US president Donald Trump’s second term. NBC News did not mince words in an August 28 report, with graphics that spelled out the climate connection: “Past 60 Years Glacial Loss increased 4X, Glaciers Less Stable Worldwide From Melting.” Even CBS News has noted, more than once, the climate connection to the Nepal disaster. This despite a president, Bari Weiss, who has fired the entire CBS News climate unit, derided climate change in newsroom meetings as “woke,” and intervened to push the network’s reporting to the right on a range of topics, above all Israel. Referring to the “glacial burst” that triggered the gargantuan flood that swept away buildings, roads, and bridges, the CBS Evening News stated on August 26 that, “Experts believe this is linked to climate change.” On August 31, CBS’s morning news show interviewed scientist Daniel Swain while graphics told viewers, “Climate Change Impacting Extreme Weather Events, Shifting Global Sea Levels, Ecosystems, and Human Health.” The Nepal coverage has demonstrated the importance of public officials speaking plainly, thus giving journalists a peg to make the climate connection to extreme events. Each of the Big Three US networks, CNN, the BBC, and other international news organizations headlined the statement by Nepal’s foreign minister, Shisir Kahnal, blaming the flooding on global warming. Days later, Kahnal said that Nepal is demanding compensation from the world’s biggest emitters. Such high-profile coverage predictably irritated the tiny but noisy band of bots and cheery-picking blowhards who still deny climate change. The opinion section of The Wall Street Journal, which has disparaged climate science since the 1990s, published an article on August 28 that studiously avoided engaging with the actual scientific expertise other outlets had cited. Instead, it accused “the Western media” of rushing to judgment by embracing its “all-purpose explanation for everything: climate change.” The Journal’s accusation was hardly more persuasive than that of an online conspiracy theorist who tried to blame the Nepal floods on a research project in Alaska. The fact checking unit of AFP, which delivers news to thousands of news outlets and government offices worldwide, quickly slapped down that absurdity: “AFP has repeatedly debunked claims that the High-frequency Active Auroral Research Program (HAARP) is to blame for extreme weather events, and scientists say manipulation cannot cause floods of this magnitude — instead pointing to human-caused global warming.” Why the Nepal disaster has called forth more plainspoken climate coverage than usual is, at this point, unclear. The availability of stunning video showing the awesome size, speed, and force of the flood was doubtless a factor. But that can’t be the sole explanation: The images of Helene’s ferocious winds and of Los Angeles hillsides engulfed in flames were no less eye-catching. Yes, the link between higher global temperatures and melting glaciers makes intuitive sense, but is it any more intuitive than the connection between higher temperatures and the extreme heat that has killed 35,000 people and counting in Europe this summer? In any case, the question now is where climate coverage goes from here. Nepal’s floods are a textbook illustration of the stark injustice at the heart of the climate story: The people who did the least to cause the problem tend to be the ones who suffer the first and worst. As Bill McKibben noted on his Substack, “The Crucial Years,” “on average, Nepalis produce about four-tenths of a ton of carbon emissions annually, compared with about 14 tons for an American.” At the COP28 UN climate summit in 2023, the world’s governments operationalized a Loss and Damage Fund to compensate victims of climate disasters. Contributions have been paltry, but The Nation reported this week that the fund’s board of governors was discussing whether to make an inaugural donation to Nepal as a symbol of why the fund needs to be fully capitalized. As journalists and newsrooms prepare to cover the COP31 summit in Turkey this November, the long-standing debate around climate loss and damage deserves our focused attention. Nepal’s floods also highlight another aspect of the climate story: Who is responsible for all those losses, and who should pay for the damages? To date, most reporting has trod lightly on these questions, even though a handful of investigative exposés have made clear who the chief culprits are. “A 1981 internal memo written by the director of one of Exxon’s science labs said it was ‘distinctly possible’ that cumulative carbon emissions could eventually ‘produce effects which will indeed be catastrophic (at least for a substantial portion of the earth’s population),” author Jeff Goodell pointed out the day after the Nepal floods. Exxon and other companies hid that science for decades, instead pressing for ever-increasing fossil fuel production and consumption. If holding power to account is a core duty of journalism, then connecting the dots between Big Oil and the Nepal floods, and other coming disasters that Big Oil’s delaying tactics have made inevitable, is a good place to start.
