title: The water beneath is running out
author: Abdur Razzaq
description: Water crises due to falling water table in the Mazdoor Abad area of KP turns daily life into a daily struggle
text: Haidar Ali, 35, a resident of Mazdoor Abad locality in Takht Bhai tehsil of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, some 15 kilometres north of Mardan city, starts his day by searching for water for drinking and household use. He and other locals collect water with great difficulty for their daily needs. A water tanker supplied them water on alternate days, giving one barrel per house which hardly met their requirements. If Ali and his family needed more water, he had to bring it by rickshaw at Rs 400 to 500 per trip. This area is located beneath the mountains where the UNESCO World Heritage Site, the Takht Bhai Buddhist Monastery, is situated. According to local residents, the groundwater level has been declining here every year, for more than a decade. Water has already depleted in Cheena Korona and Shaheen Town of the locality and the same problem is now emerging in other neighbourhoods as well. Pointing to some already locked houses in Cheena Korona and Shaheen Town, Ali said that due to water scarcity, a number of families had migrated from the area to other villages of Takht Bhai tehsil. Likewise, he and his two brothers were also planning to sell their houses and move to an area with a higher groundwater table, as life where they were presently living had become difficult with the passage of time because of the water situation. More than a decade ago, the groundwater table was about 65 feet below the surface, but it has now dropped to around 350 feet, says local political figure Hussain Yousafzai, adding that in past, people used water obtained through wells, and later they depended on tube wells established by the public health department. In the current worst situation a local philanthropist had donated a tractor and a water tanker to the community. “Most residents of the locality are poor, and keep water drums, and buckets outside their homes,” he explains. “The water tanker goes door to door and supplies water to each household.” To a query, he said that out of four water supply schemes, only two were functional and hardly met the needs of a few households located at lower altitude. Since the houses situated at a higher elevation are not able to obtain water from these schemes, the local community depended on water tankers for their water supply. "Some people store rainwater for washing clothes and other daily household needs," he added. Mazdoor Abad, a settlement in the Takht Bhai tehsil of Mardan district with a population of more than 20,000, is not the only locality facing water scarcity. An electrical resistivity survey conducted by the Public Health Engineering Department, Mardan, at different points in Mazdoor Abad, to assess groundwater potential, reveals the static water level at Point-1 to be approximately 40 feet below the ground surface, with a proposed drilling depth of around 200 feet. The estimated discharge was 3,000 gallons per hour (GPH). At Point-2, the static water level was estimated at around 20 feet, with a proposed drilling depth of approximately 200 feet and an estimated discharge of 3,000 GPH. However, the survey concluded that neither site was feasible for tubewell construction because bedrock was encountered at a shallow depth. Regarding the survey conducted in the area, Mohsin Iqbal, SDO, Public Health Engineering Department, told The Express Tribune that low yield tubewells serving two to three houses could be successful, where a limited quantity of water would be used. But a tubewell for the entire community in Mazdoor Abad would not be successful. “The water supplied to the area through pipelines came from nearby villages, where the water table is relatively high and the discharge capacity is around 5,000 to 6,000 gallons per hour (GPH),” he said. “Due to changes in precipitation patterns and the amount of rainfall, the water table varies at different times. He added that the department does not have specific data on it as the groundwater table has not been measured at different time intervals. Iqbal explained that the department did not have any tubewells in the locality. However, due to rapid population growth and the adverse impacts of climate change, the water table has declined over time. “Now the department has shifted its focus from tubewells to surface water,” he added, talking about a mega water supply scheme that has been approved for Mazdoor Abad. “We are working on its design and preparing a proposal under which surface water from the Jalala river will be pumped to a treatment plant. The treated water will be supplied to the locality. This is a shift towards surface water. Similar strategies have already been successfully implemented in Batkhela, Kohat and Karak districts of KP.” Other parts of Mardan district are also grappling with water shortages, while the declining groundwater table is becoming a concern in Peshawar and several southern and other districts of KP as well. Documents submitted by the Ministry of Water Resources to the Senate in 2021 revealed that groundwater levels were depleting rapidly in 28 districts of KP. In five districts, the water shortage was particularly alarming, with groundwater levels falling by between 25 and 74 feet over the previous decade. According to the Ministry's written reply, Khyber district was the worst affected, where the groundwater level had fallen by 74 feet, followed by Haripur with a decline of 62 feet. Mohmand ranked third, with 57 feet drop, while Bajaur ranked fourth. Kurram was fifth, where the groundwater level had dropped by 26 feet. The water scarcity issue is not only confined to several districts of KP, but the situation is becoming worse across the country. According to a report by the Asian Development Bank, Asian Water Development Outlook 2025, Pakistan remains a severely water-stressed country and facing rising pressure on its water resources due to rapid population growth, climate change and poor water management. The report says per capita water availability has declined from 3,500 cubic metres in 1972 to just 1,100 cubic metres in 2020, far below the minimum safe threshold of 1,700 cubic metres. It also states that more than 80 percent of the country's population lacks access to safely managed drinking water, increasing the risk of waterborne diseases. According to the annual 2023-24 report of Pakistan Council of Research in Water Resources (PCRWR), groundwater levels in Balochistan have been depleting at alarming rates, with declines of up to five meters annually in some regions of the province. Media reports suggested that the Punjab province groundwater table is declining at rate of 0.5 to 1.0 meters annually. The depletion is associated with the unchecked installation of tube wells which were 4500 in 1960 and in 2024 reached 1.5 million. Talking to The Express Tribune, Islamabad based water and climate change expert, Shahid Iqbal said that four divisions of KP including Mardan, Peshawar, Bannu and Dera Ismail Khan were facing more water scarcity. He added that some parts of Mardan city were experiencing water shortages, and some nearby areas were suffering from waterlogging as well. “In Mardan and Peshawar divisions, rapid population growth, increased extraction of underground freshwater has led to amplified water consumption, while the expansion of concrete infrastructure has reduced groundwater recharge during rainfall, causing the water table to gradually decline,” explains Iqbal. “In the southern region, Bannu, Karak, and Dera Ismail Khan, the situation is even worse due to the adverse impacts of climate change. It is alarming that despite the Kabul River flowing through the Peshawar and Mardan divisions, these areas are still facing water scarcity.” Highlighting how in the past, rainfall occurred at regular intervals, allowing groundwater to recharge over time, Iqbal said, “However, climate change has transformed both the pattern and intensity of precipitation. As a result, groundwater is no longer being recharged as effectively as it was more than a decade ago. This is one of the main reasons our region is grappling with water scarcity.” Iqbal explained that the quantity of rainfall that used to occur in 10 days now often falls in a single day with higher intensity, causing urban flooding instead of recharging the groundwater table. “In such a situation, how can rainwater be properly absorbed into the ground, especially when most of the land is covered with concrete buildings and only limited areas are available for water harvesting?” According to an estimate, in Peshawar’s posh areas, including Hayatabad, Regi Lalma, University Town and the old walled city, the water table has been falling by three to four inches annually, which is a significant decline, he mentioned, as he recalled that in 1990, the water table in Hayatabad was about 300 feet below ground level, but it has now fallen to around 500 to 550 feet which is a huge drop in more than two three decades. Professor Dr Muhammad Nafees, a faculty member in the Department of Environmental Sciences at the University of Peshawar revealed that in Pakistan, almost 90 percent of water was extracted from groundwater resources, while 10 percent came from surface water. He added that the unchecked use of water for household and commercial purposes through a large number of water pumps and tube wells had contributed to water scarcity in the country. "The main reason for groundwater depletion is that water is being extracted faster than it can be recharged. In the past, rainfall occurred at regular intervals and with balanced intensity, allowing groundwater to recharge naturally. However, due to climate change and the expansion of concrete infrastructure, the recharge process has been disrupted. As a result, less rainwater seeps into the ground, while most of it flows into canals and rivers,” says Professor Nafees, adding that in Pakistan, annual groundwater recharge was about 55 billion cubic metres, while annual extraction had reached 65 billion cubic metres, hence as a result, around 10 billion cubic metres more water was extracted. He suggested that protecting water resources required creating public awareness about reducing water consumption and avoiding the wastage of this precious natural resource. “If water was used responsibly, the groundwater table could gradually recover, while rainwater harvesting at the household, village, and town levels through storage tanks, ponds, and small dams was also crucial for recharging and safeguarding groundwater resources.” To reduce the hardships faced by residents of Mazdoor Abad, Haidar Ali urged the provincial government and the relevant departments to make the available tube wells functional as a short-term relief measure. He also called on the authorities to devise a mechanism to address the issue of groundwater depletion in the locality, this way further migration from the area could be prevented. title: Pakistan Air Force in the crucible of 1965
author: Izmi Herlani
description: Remembering the September sacrifice
text: There are moments in a nation’s history when dates cease to be dates and become moments reliving a turning point in the fate of the country. September 6, 1965 was one such moment for Pakistan. Guns roared along the frontier. Armoured columns moved toward Lahore. Across the country, uncertainty turned into fear as the reality of war sank in. Pakistan stood before a formidable challenge and the battlefield was no longer confined to the ground. Above it all stretched the sky and into that sky rose the Shaheens of Pakistan Air Force. When Indian forces attempted to cross the international border on September 6, 1965, Pakistan Air Force did not have the luxury of numbers. Its resources were limited, its aircraft finite and its pilots painfully aware that every sortie could be their last. But there are things no inventory can measure: training, discipline, leadership, courage and the unyielding will to fight for one’s country. For the Men in Blues, the cockpit was not merely a place from which to fly, it was where duty became destiny. The call came—and they answered. F-86 Sabres thundered from their dispersals. B-57 bombers disappeared into the darkness. Air-defence units watched the skies with relentless vigilance. Fighter pilots climbed toward an enemy that possessed numerical strength, knowing that somewhere beneath them were cities, soldiers, families and millions of civilians depending upon their ability to hold the line. The battle for Pakistan’s skies had begun. The aerial war of 1965 was fought at terrifying speed and merciless altitude. Aircraft met over the plains of Punjab. Guns flashed, missiles and cannon fire tore through the air, pilots manoeuvred within seconds of life and death knowing that one mistake could mean a fiery descent from the sky. There was no time for hesitation, only instinct. Among the men who entered that inferno was Squadron Leader Sarfaraz Ahmed Rafiqui Shaheed—a name that would become synonymous with sacrifice. On September 6, Rafiqui led his formation against the heavily defended Halwara airfield. Enemy fighters rose to meet them and the sky erupted into a furious contest of skill and nerve. Then disaster struck. Rafiqui’s guns jammed. His aircraft could no longer deliver fire effectively. Yet he did not turn away from the battle. He remained in the combat zone, continuing to engage the enemy and drawing attention away from his fellow pilots. He had lost the ability to fight but he had not lost the ability to lead. In those final moments, Rafiqui placed the survival of his men above his own. He did not return. His aircraft fell beyond the border but the man inside it rose to be a legend. That is what makes Rafiqui’s story so profoundly moving. He sacrificed his tomorrow so that others could have theirs. That is leadership stripped of rank, ceremony and glory. That is sacrifice. And then came another name that would echo through the skies of 1965: Air Commodore M M Alam. On September 7, flying his F-86 Sabre, Alam entered one of the most extraordinary aerial engagements of the war. In a breathtaking burst of combat skill, he was credited with shooting down five Indian aircraft in less than a minute making his combat tally of nine confirmed IAF killed and two damaged enemy aircraft. The circumstances were extraordinary but behind the feat stood something even more important: years of preparation compressed into seconds of decision. In the cockpit, there was no room for hesitation, no time to calculate odds. There was only the aircraft, the enemy and the instinct of a highly trained fighter pilot. For Pakistan, Alam’s achievement became more than a remarkable combat episode. It became a symbol of what PAF represented in those challenging days; a force that refused to allow numerical superiority to become psychological defeat. Yet the story of 1965 cannot belong only to the celebrated names. Behind every victorious pilot stood a fraternity of men whose names rarely appeared in headlines: the ground crew who worked through the night to return a damaged aircraft to service; the armourer loading weapons while the next sortie was already being prepared; the radar operator watching the screen for an approaching formation; the controller guiding fighters toward an unseen enemy; the technician repairing engines under the relentless pressure of wartime operations; the signals operator, the meteorologist, the maintenance crew and the countless men who kept the machines—and therefore the missions—alive. They were the invisible architecture of every aerial victory. And then there were those who returned. Some landed with aircraft scarred by enemy fire. Some climbed down from their cockpits knowing that a friend who had taken off beside them would never return. Some returned to the same runway again and again, carrying the weight of those they had lost. They were the Ghazis but alongside them stood another brotherhood—the Shaheeds. The brave men who never heard the celebrations. The valiant men who never walked back into their homes. The men whose families waited at doors that would never again open to the sound of their footsteps. Their sacrifice was not simply a military statistic, it was the price paid for sovereignty. The 1965 war demonstrated a truth that remains relevant far beyond aviation: air power is not measured merely by the number of aircraft standing on a runway. It is measured by the people who fly them, by the men who maintain them, by the commanders who make decisions when seconds matter, by the training that transforms fear into action and ultimately, by the courage to enter the sky when the safest choice would be to remain on the ground. Pakistan Air Force entered the 1965 war facing a formidable numerical challenge. Yet its air warriors refused to allow numbers to determine the outcome of their spirit. They flew, they fought, they endured. And some gave everything. Six decades later, the sound of those Sabres and bombers may have faded from the skies, the runways have changed, the uniforms have evolved, the aircraft of that era now belong to history but the spirit of those brave men does not belong to history. It belongs to Pakistan. It lives in the name of Rafiqui, who chose his formation over his own life. It lives in the memory of M M Alam, whose extraordinary combat performance became part of the nation’s military heritage. It lives in every technician who worked through the darkness, every pilot who climbed into danger and every Shaheed who never came home. Perhaps that is the most enduring legacy of September 1965: When the nation looked toward the sky, it did not see machines, it saw men who had decided that the sky would not be surrendered. They left behind something greater than victory—a legacy of courage written not in ink but in fire across the September sky. The aircraft are gone, the battles are over, the men have passed into history but the sky still remembers.

title: Islamabad ATC grants bail to Mushtaq Ahmad, 95 others over AJK protest
author: Fiaz Mahmood
description: Former senator faces charges under provisions of PPC, Peaceful Assembly, Public Order Act, Anti-Terrorism Act
text: An Islamabad anti-terrorism court (ATC) on Monday granted post-arrest bail to former senator Mushtaq Ahmad Khan and 95 others in a case registered over a protest concerning Azad Jammu and Kashmir (AJK) in Islamabad’s Sector F-10. ATC Judge Abual Hasnat Muhammad Zulqarnain heard the bail applications, while prosecutor Raja Naveed Hussain Kiani appeared on behalf of the prosecution. Defence lawyers, including Sardar Masroof, Zahid Bashir Dar and Amina Ali, represented the suspects. After hearing arguments from both sides, the court approved bail for all 96 suspects against surety bonds of Rs5,000 each. The case was registered at Shalimar Police Station under provisions of the Anti-Terrorism Act in connection with the protest. Ahmad was initially detained on July 30 after security personnel stopped him from entering Azad Jammu and Kashmir. His team alleged that he was held for more than 24 hours because he supported the ongoing protests in the region. After his release, Ahmad returned to Islamabad and announced the gathering at F-10 Markaz, inviting the public, student organisations, journalists and Kashmiris living in the capital. In a video message, he said the event would be a gathering for “sympathy, affection, peace and reconciliation” for Kashmir. The gathering later led to the registration of a case at Islamabad’s Shalimar Police Station against Ahmad and other protesters. According to the FIR, registered on July 31 on the complaint of police officer Ghulam Murtaza, the protesters had gathered at F-10 Markaz and allegedly blocked roads, resisted police and created a law-and-order situation. Read: Islamabad ATC extends former senator Mushtaq Ahmad's physical remand by four days The FIR named Ahmad among the accused and alleged that his speeches had contributed to the crowd’s actions and that protesters had resisted police attempts to clear the area. The case included Sections 324, 395, 342, 341, 427/440, 506(ii), 109, 188, 353, 186, 148 and 149 of the Pakistan Penal Code, as well as Sections 2/3 of the Peaceful Assembly and Public Order Act 2024 and Section 7 of the Anti-Terrorism Act. Police alleged in the FIR that the protesters had continued their activities despite attempts by law-enforcement personnel to control the situation. The accused were initially granted three days’ physical remand on August 3 after the court rejected the prosecution’s request for 30 days. The remand was later extended by four days on August 6. Prosecutors had argued that investigators needed further custody to recover a vehicle and weapons allegedly linked to the case. Ahmad had previously drawn nationwide attention after being detained by Israeli forces while aboard the Global Sumud Flotilla, a humanitarian mission carrying food and medicine to Gaza. Leading a five-member Pakistani delegation, his detention prompted widespread concern in Pakistan, with the Foreign Office saying it had worked "tirelessly" to secure his safe evacuation through Pakistan's embassy in Jordan. After his release, he returned to Islamabad to a hero's welcome, where he was received by supporters at the airport.

title: Republicans are making Muslims a campaign issue in the 2026 US midterms
author: Reuters
description: Over the past year, Muslims have gained more political power than at any point in recent memory
text: United States Vice President JD Vance called Abdul El-Sayed, a Muslim and a Democrat running for the US Senate in Michigan, "very, very evil" at a rally last week, accusing him of defending terrorism because of remarks he made after a March attack on a suburban Detroit synagogue. In Texas, Republican Governor Greg Abbott, in a close race for another term, attacked a proposed Muslim-led development and called for an investigation into what he described as efforts to create “sharia courts”, a claim disputed by developers and civil rights groups. In Alabama, where Muslims make up less than half a per cent of the population, US Senator Tommy Tuberville, a Republican running for governor, warned that “the enemy is inside the gates”, referring to what he called radical Islam. Sen. Tommy Tuberville (R-Alabama), who is running for governor of his state, shared a post on X attacking New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani (D). Tuberville has repeatedly made anti-Muslim attacks against Mamdani. https://t.co/v4WBO5J4Xq — The Washington Post (@washingtonpost) March 13, 2026 Muslims become a campaign issue The comments reflect an effort to make Muslims and Islam part of the election debate ahead of the November 3 midterms that will determine whether Democrats can wrest control of Congress from President Donald Trump's Republican Party. Critics say the rhetoric unfairly targets Muslims, while Republicans say they are raising legitimate concerns about security, extremism and the role of religion in public life. Abbott campaign spokesman Eduardo Leal said the Texas governor's actions regarding the development were aimed at alleged illegal conduct, not religious beliefs. Muslims number about 5.5 million people in the United States, up from 2.4 million in 2007, according to Pew Research Centre. They account for about 1.6% of the country's population. Over the past year, Muslims have gained more political power than at any point in recent memory. New York City elected its first Muslim mayor, Zohran Mamdani, while El-Sayed could become the first Muslim senator. Last year, Ghazala Hashmi became the first Muslim woman elected to a statewide office when she became Virginia's lieutenant governor. The rhetoric has spread to House races as well. Read: Anti-Muslim hate targeting Michigan Senate nominee El-Sayed surged after primary win: study Republican Representatives Keith Self and Chip Roy, both of Texas, have organised a "Sharia Free America Caucus", and Republican Representative Randy Fine of Florida has introduced legislation that he says will "tackle the rise" of sharia law in the United States. 🚨Reps. Roy, Self Launch Sharia Free America Caucus: Washington, D.C. -- Representatives Chip Roy (TX-21) and Keith Self (TX-03) officially launched the Sharia-Free America Caucus in the House of Representatives, an effort to counter the alarming rise of Sharia Law in the United… — Rep. Chip Roy Press Office (@RepChipRoy) December 18, 2025 Aides to Fine did not respond to requests for comment. El-Sayed at centre of debate As the only Muslim running for statewide office in the country, the American-born El-Sayed has been the focus of anti-Islamic rhetoric around the country. Vance's criticism centred on comments El-Sayed made after a man drove a vehicle into a suburban Detroit synagogue in March while children were in the building. El-Sayed condemned the attack but also said of the assailant that "hurt people hurt people", noting that some of the man's relatives in Lebanon had recently been killed in an Israeli airstrike. El-Sayed later said the remarks may have been misconstrued and apologised. In response to Vance's attack, El-Sayed said last month: "Evil is ripping healthcare away from working people in exchange for tax breaks for billionaires. Evil is making people pay more for groceries and gas while pushing for trade wars and actual war. Evil is dividing people for your own gain." El-Sayed has faced Republican criticism for associating with Hasan Piker, a left-wing social media influencer who has said the United States deserved the September 11, 2001, attacks. In a podcast interview, El-Sayed discussed the feelings of isolation some Americans experience, which he blamed on cellphones and social media, and contrasted it with the sense of community his relatives in Egypt enjoy. In response, Tuberville posted on X, “If you hate America so much, go live in Egypt.” Abdul El-Sayed thinks America is to blame for the 9/11 Islamic terrorist attacks. He doesn’t belong within 1,000 miles of the U.S. Senate. — Coach Tommy Tuberville (@SenTuberville) September 1, 2026 Aides to the Tuberville campaign did not respond to requests for comment. Debate over political motives The public has doubts about Trump, whose approval rating is stuck at around 33%. Their top concerns: the high cost of living, the US-Israeli war on Iran and Trump's tariffs on foreign goods. Public attitudes towards Israel have shifted, particularly among Democrats, with polls showing growing sympathy for Palestinians and increasing opposition to US military aid. Aaron Hughes, a University of Rochester religious studies professor and scholar of Islam and Judaism, said the increased focus on Muslims comes as Republicans struggle to gain political traction on issues such as the cost of living, the Iran war and immigration. "If you can wrap yourself in the flag and you can criticise Muslims and Islam, that means you don't really have to deal with the issues," he said in a telephone interview, calling it "fear-mongering". "You're taking this gross characterisation of a community and making connections with Hamas, with Iran ... I find it most shocking that there's this conflation," he said. The rhetorical attacks occur, Hughes noted, despite many Muslims holding conservative beliefs that dovetail with Republican orthodoxy, such as opposition to some abortion procedures and same-sex marriage. There is a history in the United States of targeting minorities in political campaigns, but the rhetoric has become sharper, according to experts. Read More: Muslim American groups say Republicans are weaponising congressional hearings Exactly two years ago, some Republicans running for public office, including Trump, spread the false claim that immigrant Haitians living in the small town of Springfield, Ohio, were eating pets. "They're eating the dogs! The people that came in. They're eating the cats! They're eating ... the pets of the people that live there," Trump said in a 2024 presidential debate. While Trump is not on the ballot, the public's low support for his performance could be a drag on his fellow Republicans. Ashik Siddique, co-chair of the Democratic Socialists of America, said it would be wrong to hang Islamophobia on just one political party. "Unfortunately, sometimes Democrats in leadership have also fed into this anti-Islamic rhetoric, he said. He was referring to a radio interview Andrew Cuomo did last October when running as an independent candidate in the New York City mayoral election before being defeated by Mamdani. "Can you imagine Mamdani in the seat during the September 11, 2001, attack? Cuomo asked the show's host. Beyond the campaign trail The issue has extended beyond the campaign trail. In August, Abbott urged a federal probe of two Texas airports over Islamic ritual washing facilities, arguing that government-owned airports could not favour one religion over another. Abbott's campaign rejected accusations that it was targeting Muslims because of their faith. Houston's Democratic Mayor John Whitmire said the airports' ablution room and adjoining prayer room are "open to all travellers, employees and stakeholders" regardless of faith and that "nobody receives preferential access, and nobody is excluded".

title: Filmmaker Tigmanshu Dhulia discusses ‘Dhurandhar’, says Indian cinema lacks strong storylines
author: Life And Style Desk
description: Argues industry was changing due to growing influence of corporate culture
text: Indian filmmaker Tigmanshu Dhulia questioned the state of storytelling in the country's cinema, citing Dhurandhar as a prime example of the industry’s transition towards fictional biopics. According to Gulf News, Dhulia discussed Dhurandhar's execution, describing it as engaging. However, he argued that it didn't have an underlying plot in the traditional sense. Instead, it followed a commercially driven fictional-biopic format. “There is a man, he is a cover spy. He goes to Pakistan and wreaks havoc there,” Dhulia said. “Is that a story? Stories have disappeared from films.” The filmmaker compared the approach to other commercially successful films such as Pushpa and KGF, arguing that they followed a similar template. Dhulia added that the industry was changing because of the growing influence of corporate culture, with filmmakers increasingly relying on familiar formulas. “They are not allowed to tell those stories because they think, ‘These stories won’t work.’ There is only one template,” he said. The filmmaker also spoke about the growing sameness of popular culture around the world, suggesting that even cities and their individual identities were increasingly becoming indistinguishable. “Go anywhere, everybody looks the same. Every city has started looking the same. The character of every city has disappeared,” he said. Using his hometown as an example, Dhulia told Gulf News that it had also lost some of its distinctive character. “My city, Allahabad, which was once a beautiful city, now looks like any other city. The same malls, the same cars, everything is the same,” he said. Dhurandhar is an undercover Indian intelligence operative film written and produced by Aditya Dhar. The film features Ranveer Singh, Akshaye Khanna and Sanjay Dutt, among other notable faces from the Indian entertainment industry. According to Gulf News, Dhurandhar grossed over Rs3 billion worldwide, becoming one of Bollywood's biggest commercial films. Dhulia questioned the same success due to what he saw as the lack of a proper storyline.

title: Netanyahu warned by UAE president before October 7 events, failed to brief security chiefs: Haaretz
author: Anadolu Agency
description: Former Prime Minister Naftali Bennett says warning to Netanyahu ‘true,’ accuses him of ‘criminal negligence’
text: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu received an “explicit warning” from the United Arab Emirates about Hamas plans to carry out a major attack before the October 7, 2023 events, but he failed to brief Israel’s security chiefs, Haaretz reported on Tuesday. The Israeli daily said UAE President Sheikh Mohamed bin Zayed held a 45-minute phone conversation with Netanyahu about a week and a half before October 7, warning him that Hamas leader Yahya Sinwar was preparing a major operation against Israel. Haaretz, which based its report on dozens of Israeli and foreign sources as well as recordings, internal documents and correspondence, said the UAE president urged Netanyahu to take the threat seriously. The Israeli premier reportedly responded that he believed Hamas intended to carry out an operation in the occupied West Bank and assured bin Zayed that Israel was prepared for any scenario. Despite the warning, Netanyahu did not brief the heads of the Shin Bet domestic security agency, Mossad intelligence agency or the Israeli army chief of staff about his conversation with the UAE president, according to the report. Read: Israeli clearance of Gaza rubble could destroy genocide evidence A senior Shin Bet official cited by Haaretz said that knowing about the warnings “could have changed our entire assessment picture.” Haaretz claimed that bin Zayed later told then-CIA Director William Burns about his concerns and the message he had conveyed to Netanyahu that “something there is about to explode.” According to the newspaper, the warning from the UAE president was not the first indication Israeli authorities had received about Hamas plans. The report said a Palestinian intermediary had conveyed a message from Sinwar in September 2023 that he was preparing a “huge surprise” and an “earthquake.” The warning was passed to the Shin Bet on September 15, prompting then-Shin Bet chief Ronen Bar to brief Netanyahu and leading to subsequent security discussions, according to the daily. Haaretz also cited a similar warning reportedly delivered to Netanyahu’s office by then-Egyptian intelligence chief Abbas Kamel about “something unusual” being prepared by Hamas. Netanyahu’s office strongly denied receiving any warning from the UAE leader. “Prime Minister Netanyahu didn’t speak to the president of the UAE during the period in question and received no warning from him,” it said, calling the Haaretz report an “absolute lie.” Former Shin Bet chief Bar and former Israeli army chief Herzl Halevi said they had not been informed of the warning allegedly delivered by bin Zayed, according to Haaretz. There was no immediate comment from the UAE on the report. For his part, former Prime Minister Naftali Bennett said the Haaretz report about the warning was “true,” accusing Netanyahu of “criminal negligence” for failing to act on the warnings. “Netanyahu bears personal and direct responsibility for the failure that led to the deaths of thousands of Israelis on his watch,” Bennett said on US social media company X. Read more: Houthi attacks wound 73, disrupt Saudi energy facilities as group warns of more strikes inside kingdom Opposition politician and former Israeli army chief Gadi Eisenkot similarly accused Netanyahu of ignoring repeated warnings. “Netanyahu received dozens of warnings ahead of Oct. 7 and ignored them all. He is unfit,” Eisenkot said. On October 8, 2023, the Israeli army launched a brutal offensive on Gaza that has killed more than 73,000 people, injured over 174,000 and destroyed much of the territory’s civilian infrastructure.

title: UN commission says Israeli attacks on southern Syria ‘must stop’
author: Anadolu Agency
description: Body expresses ‘deep concern,’ says attacks violate country’s sovereignty, territorial integrity
text: The United Nations Independent International Commission of Inquiry on Syria on Tuesday expressed “deep concern” over Israeli attacks on southern Syria, saying they violate the country’s sovereignty and territorial integrity and “must stop.” The commission made the call during a briefing to the UN Human Rights Council, whose 63rd regular session began in Geneva on Monday and runs through October 7. “We are deeply concerned about the Israeli attacks on southern Syria and affirm that they constitute a violation of its sovereignty and territorial integrity,” the commission said, according to Syria’s SANA news agency. “This is unacceptable and must stop,” it added. Areas of southern Syria, particularly Quneitra and Daraa provinces, have witnessed repeated Israeli military incursions, including raids on homes, the establishment of checkpoints and arrests, as well as shelling. Read: IAEA finds tonnes of nuclear material in Syria Israel has occupied most of the Syrian Golan Heights since 1967. Following the fall of the Bashar al-Assad regime on December 8, 2024, Israel declared the 1974 Separation of Forces Agreement collapsed and occupied the demilitarised buffer zone and other positions, including the Syrian side of Mount Hermon (Jabal al-Sheikh). On developments inside Syria, the commission said it was witnessing an acceleration in reconstruction and progress in efforts to build accountability institutions. It stressed that “accountability is an essential element for the success of the transitional justice process in Syria.” Read More: Syria mulls joining Makkah pact The commission also welcomed the renewal of its mandate and thanked the Syrian government for enabling it to carry out its work. The UN Human Rights Council established the Independent International Commission of Inquiry on Syria in August 2011 to investigate alleged violations of international human rights law since March that year and identify those responsible where possible. For years, the commission conducted its investigations from outside Syria because it lacked access to the country, relying on interviews with victims and witnesses as well as documents, photographs, videos and satellite imagery.

title: KU senior professor allegedly assaulted, detained after minor traffic dispute
author: Sajid Rauf
description: Arif Saqi alleges the perpetrator fired shots into the air, attacked him with the butt of a pistol
text: Dr Professor Arif Khan Saqi, chairman of the University of Karachi’s (UoK) Islamic Learning Department, was allegedly severely assaulted and held against his will following a minor traffic dispute near Safoora Chowrangi in Karachi on Tuesday, with police saying gunmen employed by the son of a restaurant owner were involved in the incident. In a video statement, Dr Saqi said he was travelling from his home to the university after booking an online motorcycle ride when the confrontation began outside Sindh Green Restaurant near Rim Jhim Tower. He said that a vehicle was coming out of the restaurant to join the road when a security guard came out and signalled for them to stop. They stopped, but the vehicle then reversed at speed and hit their motorcycle. The driver began to leave the scene, prompting Saqi to intervene and ask for compensation for the damage to the motorcycle. “I told him that the online bike rider was a poor man who was using someone else’s motorcycle to earn his livelihood and could not afford to bear the cost of the damage. I asked that whatever damage has been caused should be compensated,” he said. It was at this point, Saqi alleged, that the dispute escalated. He said that the son of the restaurant owner came outside, fired shots into the air and attacked him with the butt of a pistol. Saqi alleged that he and the motorcycle rider were dragged inside the hotel, where their mobile phones were taken from them and later returned. title: 25 years after 9/11, Americans fear domestic extremists more than foreign attacks
author: Reuters
description: Poll says 61% see domestic extremists as bigger threat than foreign groups, up sharply from views decade ago
text: Twenty-five years after the September 11 attacks focused United States fears on threats from abroad, Americans are now considerably more worried about attacks by domestic extremists than by foreign groups, a Reuters/Ipsos poll found. When asked to name the biggest threat to the safety of average Americans, 33% of respondents picked "domestic terrorism," while 20% picked foreign terror and 42% pointed to random acts of violence such as mass shootings, the August 28-31 poll found. The picture was much different a decade ago. Reuters/Ipsos polling from mid-2013 showed 21% of Americans viewed domestic terror as the top threat, less than the 28% who pointed to foreign terror and 51% who picked random acts of violence. Foreign al Qaeda militants crashed airplanes into New York City's World Trade Centre and the Pentagon outside Washington on September 11, 2001, killing thousands and sparking decades of war, including the US-led invasion of Afghanistan, where al Qaeda leaders were based. Al Qaeda also inspired the 2013 Boston Marathon bombing, in which a pair of foreign-born brothers killed three and injured more than 260, with a fourth person killed a few days later. Fears of domestic extremism But the US has also seen many domestically inspired attacks, including the 2016 mass shooting that killed 49 people at a Florida gay nightclub and other attacks on Black, Latino or Jewish Americans. President Donald Trump himself faced multiple assassination attempts, including a 2024 shooting that wounded his ear, and conservative activist Charlie Kirk was gunned down in September 2025 while speaking to university students in Utah. Asked which ideology-driven attacks pose the bigger threat, 61% of respondents in the latest poll picked domestic extremists and 34% picked those from abroad. The legacy of the September 11 attacks remains strong, the survey found. Six in 10 people say they periodically think about the attacks and roughly the same share say they would support a military response if there were another major attack. Read: Independent voters shift toward Democrats ahead of US midterms: poll But Americans do not believe that wars that followed 9/11 were worth the cost. Some 48% said the war in Afghanistan was not worth its toll, compared with 21% who said it was, while the rest were unsure or didn't answer the question. The war in Iraq was similarly unpopular, with 51% disapproving and 21% approving. Public disapproval of those wars played a role in Trump's rise, as he campaigned on a platform of avoiding enduring wars. Trump himself launched a war on Iran six months ago that has eluded efforts for a speedy resolution. The poll found only 25% of Americans think the conflict has been worth it, compared with 54% who think it hasn't been. Support for increased security Six in 10 Americans - including eight in 10 Republicans - think the US government response to the September 11 attacks has been at least somewhat effective in preventing attacks against Americans on US soil. A bipartisan majority - including 71% of Democrats and 75% of Republicans - think the beefed-up airport security that took hold following the September 11 attacks has been worth the disruptions to people's trips. Americans are also more inclined to support government-run airport security, with only 23% supporting an idea studied by the Trump administration that would replace federal security with private contractors. 48% were opposed, the poll found. The expansion of domestic surveillance after 2001 has been less popular, with 65% opposed to allowing US intelligence agencies to monitor electronic communications of US citizens without a warrant. A 2008 law that allowed that to happen lapsed in June, though the Trump administration has asked Congress to reauthorise the practice. Most Americans look back on September 11 as an event that unified the country, and 75% of the country thinks it had a major impact on the nation, far more than the 41% who think the 2007-2009 financial crisis had a major impact. The Reuters/Ipsos poll, which was conducted online, surveyed 1,167 US adults nationwide, with margins of error between three and six percentage points.

title: Teen reading slumps to worst this century due to surge in screen time
author: Reuters
description: On average, students were reading at a level that had in the past been expected of students one year younger
text: Teenagers more accustomed to smartphones than Shakespeare are reading at the worst levels seen this century, driving a broader decline in education, a global student assessment found. The Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development's 2025 test of 760,000 15-year-olds across 91 countries showed reading, mathematics and science scores at their lowest levels since data began to be collected in 2000. On average, students were reading at a level that had in the past been expected of students one year younger, according to the OECD's latest Programme for International Student Assessment released on Tuesday. A 2012 reading high of 501 on PISA's index had declined to a score of 466 last year. The test is widely regarded as the world's leading gauge of educational performance, and its results are closely scrutinised by governments and educators. "In reading, more screen time and less reading for pleasure have gone hand in hand with weaker results," OECD head Mathias Cormann told a press conference. "We're also seeing more hasty reading, students rushing through a text and giving a quick wrong answer." Reading scores fell more sharply in students from better-off backgrounds, the study added. Hindered by falling reading standards, average teenage science and maths skills were also at their lowest this century. Science fell from a 2009 high of 506 on the index to 486, while maths was down from 502 to 469 in the same period. Read: US sanctions threaten to crush Iranian students' dreams East Asia was the best-performing region. Chinese cities that participated in the test, Japan, Korea, Singapore and Taiwan had the best educational systems, with Britain and Estonia the only countries outside the region that made it into the top 10 in reading, mathematics and science. Digital distraction The report stopped short of endorsing smartphone bans in schools. But it said that digital distraction is linked to lower science scores in 59 of 82 education systems studied, and more than one in four students say devices distract classmates in science lessons. The OECD said students reported spending an average of 3.4 hours per weekday on digital devices for leisure in OECD member countries, and another 3 hours per weekday in the classroom and at home for learning. Digital devices could be used to improve learning, but only up to a point, Cormann said. If used more than five hours a day, results started to fall, he added. The study also found that nearly half of students use artificial intelligence chatbots regularly for learning, but those who use them for drafting essays, summarising texts and researching topics generally score about 20 points lower in science, equivalent to a year's learning.

title: Plea landed in FCC seeking ban on social media access for children under 16
author: Rana Yasif
description: Petition argues that measures are required to protect children's innocence and development
text: A plea was filed in the Federal Constitutional Court (FCC) seeking directions to the government to restrict social media access for children below 16 years of age, introduce a mandatory age-verification mechanism, and take measures to shield minors from cyberbullying, sexualised content, addiction, and other harmful material. Last week, the Punjab Assembly unanimously passed a resolution recommending measures to restrict social media access for children under the age of 16 and ensure their safety in the digital environment. The resolution recommended measures to protect children from cyber harassment, online sexual exploitation and inappropriate content. It also called for an effective age-verification mechanism on social media platforms to identify underage users. The plea sought directions to the Pakistan Electronic Media Regulatory Authority (PEMRA) to strictly enforce its Code of Conduct and prevent the airing of indecent scenes and depiction of alcohol in television dramas and advertisements during hours when children are likely to be watching. Petitioners Sheraz Zaka, Supreme Court advocate, and Ch Moien Akhtar, High Court advocate — made the Federation of Pakistan, Ministry of Information Technology, National Cyber Crime Investigation Agency (NCCIA), PEMRA and the Social Media Protection Regulatory Authority respondents. The petitioners asked the court to direct the federal government to legislate or amend the Prevention of Electronic Crimes Act (PECA), 2016, to impose restrictions on social media access for children under 16 and establish an effective age-verification system. They contended that Pakistani law presently does not specifically provide for an under-16 restriction or mandatory age verification for social media platforms. The petition pointed out that countries including Australia, Italy and Brazil had introduced restrictions on social media use by children under 16, arguing that such regulation was therefore feasible. According to the plea, children were increasingly exposed to cyberbullying, social-media addiction, sexualised content and the glorification of alcohol, which the petitioners say could adversely affect their mental and moral development. Read: Can Pakistan keep under-16s off social media? They also alleged that PEMRA failed to effectively enforce its Code of Conduct concerning television advertisements and dramas, with some programmes allegedly depicting intimate scenes and alcohol consumption at times accessible to children. The petitioners separately approached PEMRA, complaining about the alleged depiction of alcoholic drinks and intimate scenes involving young actors and actresses in certain drama serials. The petition argued that the alleged inaction of the authorities violates Articles 9, 14, 25, 25-A and 35 of the Constitution, making the matter one of public importance involving enforcement of fundamental rights and protection of the future of Pakistani youth. It also invoked the Convention on the Rights of the Child, arguing that measures are required to protect children's innocence and development. The petitioners further highlighted Pakistan's large out-of-school population, stating that around 25 million children were out of school, and had asked the court to direct the authorities to ensure that children up to the age of 16 receive education and to take measures against the high number of out-of-school children and dropout rates. Read More: Govt tightens social media rules for civil servants The plea asked the court to direct the NCCIA and the Social Media Protection Regulatory Authority to coordinate with social media platforms and introduce effective parental-control mechanisms to protect children. The petitioners also relied upon a Lahore High Court judgment, PLD 2020 Lahore 137, claiming that the court had issued directions to the state concerning legislation on human rights and social issues. The petitioners have requested the FCC to issue any other appropriate orders necessary to protect minors from harmful social media and media content. Read More: Punjab Assembly passes resolution to restrict social media access for children under 16 The resolution in the Punjab Assembly was moved by Punjab Child Protection and Welfare Bureau Chairperson and MPA Sarah Ahmed, and called for effective legislation to protect children under 16 and safeguard their digital future. It further recommended that social media companies comply with child protection standards and that a coordinated mechanism be established among federal and provincial institutions for the online protection of children. Countries around the globe, including China, the United Arab Emirates and Türkiye, have either instituted measures intended to curtail or bar access to social media for young people, or have said they were planning to do so. Last month, France's top court blocked a bill banning social media access for under-15s, saying it infringed upon freedom of expression and delivering a setback for President Emmanuel Macron, who asked his government to rewrite the legislation. Australia in December became the world's first country to ban social media for children under 16, blocking them from platforms including TikTok, YouTube and Meta's Instagram and Facebook. Also Read: France's top court blocks social media ban for under-15s The European Union said it was planning to seek stronger protections for children from harmful social media features. However, social media companies generally oppose blanket bans, saying they have measures already in place to protect younger users, including age restrictions, though they have also said they would comply with government bans. Google, Meta, Snap and TikTok did not immediately respond to requests for comment. Social media platforms including TikTok, Facebook and Snapchat say people need to be at least 13 to sign up. Child protection advocates say the controls are insufficient, and official data in several European countries shows huge numbers of children under 13 have social media accounts.

text: Indian singer-songwriter Anuv Jain recently opened up about a memorable encounter with Pakistani singing sensation Atif Aslam, recalling how a casual invitation to a barbecue (BBQ) turned into an unforgettable late-night music session. Atif performed alongside members of his band, creating a relaxed atmosphere where everyone sang and played music together. “We were sitting there for four hours. The singer's recollection highlights the informal and spontaneous nature of the evening, which he described as one of his best experiences. Rather than being a formal industry gathering, the night became an opportunity for the musicians to simply sit together, enjoy music and spend time away from the stage. Jain had also spoken about the memorable evening at the time, sharing a picture with Atif on social media. title: Afghanistan set extensive UAE cricket schedule
author: Sports Desk
description: Bangladesh, Zimbabwe tour UAE for Tests, ODIs and T20Is across two months
text: Afghanistan will host Bangladesh and Zimbabwe for an extensive international cricket programme in the United Arab Emirates during October and November, the Afghanistan Cricket Board (ACB) said on Tuesday. The schedule will begin with a one-off Test against Bangladesh from October 9-13, followed by an ODI tri-nation series involving Afghanistan, Bangladesh and Zimbabwe from October 17-23. Each team will play the other once in the three-match league phase, with the top two sides advancing to the final on October 23. Afghanistan will then face Zimbabwe in a three-match Twenty20 international series, with matches scheduled for October 27, October 29 and November 1. The two sides will conclude the programme with a two-Test series, beginning on November 5 and followed by the second Test from November 13-17. ACB Chief Executive Naseeb Khan said the programme would provide Afghanistan with valuable competition across all three formats while offering supporters an extended period of international cricket. “Playing Bangladesh and Zimbabwe across different formats will provide our players with valuable competitive opportunities,” Khan said. Bangladesh Cricket Board CEO Nizam Uddin Chowdhury said the Test against Afghanistan would give his players their first experience of red-ball cricket in the UAE. He added that Afghanistan's record in UAE conditions would provide Bangladesh with a demanding challenge, while describing the tri-nation series as a potentially competitive tournament. Zimbabwe Cricket Managing Director Givemore Makoni also welcomed the schedule, saying the ODI series would provide quality competition while the two Tests would be particularly valuable as Zimbabwe seek more regular opportunities in the longest format. The programme will strengthen cricketing ties between Afghanistan, Bangladesh and Zimbabwe while giving all three sides significant multi-format preparation. The UAE-based schedule also provides Afghanistan with a neutral venue for hosting its international commitments, with the three teams set for nearly six weeks of cricket across Tests, ODIs and T20Is.

title: Iran says US return to Islamabad pact would pave way for de-escalation
author: Reuters
description: Iran to 'defend against aggression' until aggressors 'brought to complete regret': Pezeshkian
text: Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said on Tuesday that a US return to its commitments under the Islamabad memorandum of understanding would pave the way for easing current regional tensions. Araghchi made the remarks during a phone conversation with his Japanese counterpart Toshimitsu Motegi, according to a statement by the Iranian Foreign Ministry. The two ministers discussed bilateral relations as well as the latest regional and international developments. Araghchi blamed the current tensions in the region on what he called Washington’s violation of its commitments under the Islamabad memorandum. “The solution is simple. The US side’s return to and compliance with its commitments and signature under the Islamabad memorandum will pave the way for a return to normal conditions,” he said. The Iranian minister also briefed Motegi on the latest negotiations between Iran and Oman over the Strait of Hormuz. Araghchi said the two countries had made “significant progress” in talks aimed at establishing a temporary transit route through the strait, adding that consultations would continue on mechanisms for its future management. Tokyo calls for 'maximum restraint' Motegi, for his part, expressed "deep concern" over the resumption of attacks between the US and Iran, according to a statement by Japan's Foreign Ministry. "It is important to achieve an early de-escalation of the situation and resume talks between the US and Iran as soon as possible," he said, requesting Iran to "show maximum flexibility to avoid a prolonged continuation of the current impasse." Motegi expressed "concern over Iran’s continued attacks on civilian vessels and strongly requested Iran to exercise maximum restraint," said the statement. Reiterating Japan’s position that it "is of utmost importance to restore free and safe navigation through the Strait of Hormuz without additional costs at the earliest possible date," Motegi said the future of the strait should be discussed, in accordance with international law, by the international community as a whole, including the littoral states, the states using the waterway, and the International Maritime Organisation. He called on Iran to urge the Houthi group in Yemen to "exercise restraint," and underscored the "importance of ensuring stability in the Bab el-Mandeb Strait,” explaining that Japan “would work together with the Government of Yemen to this end." The Islamabad memorandum was signed in June following mediation by Pakistan and Qatar, providing for an end to hostilities and a framework for negotiations between Tehran and Washington. Iran has accused the US of failing to implement key provisions of the understanding, including measures related to sanctions and the naval blockade, while Washington and Gulf countries have called for free and unrestricted navigation through the Strait of Hormuz. Iran and Oman have since been holding talks on a temporary transit route through the strategic waterway, with Tehran saying the arrangement would be temporary while discussions continue on a permanent mechanism. title: Pakistan reiterates support for Saudi Arabia, backs kingdom's right to defend territory after Houthi attacks
author: Web Desk
description: PM reaffirms support for kingdom's sovereignty and security, says such 'dastardly attacks' threaten innocent lives
text: Pakistan on Tuesday reaffirmed its support for Saudi Arabia, backing the kingdom’s right to take necessary measures to defend its territory and protect its citizens following recent Houthi attacks targeting civilian and economic facilities. In a statement, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs (MoFA) said Pakistan "fully supports the Kingdom’s legitimate right to take all necessary measures to defend its territory, protect its citizens and residents and safeguard its national assets against any threat." The statement came after Houthis attacked the southern Saudi cities of Abha, Khamis Mushait, Jazan and Najran, injuring 73 people, according to Saudi authorities. Women and children were among those injured, the Saudi-led coalition in Yemen said. The attacks also triggered fires at some energy facilities, where operations were subsequently halted as firefighting and emergency teams worked to contain the blazes and assess the damage. The ministry strongly condemned the "reprehensible attacks carried out by the Houthi militia" against civilian and economic targets in Abha, Khamis Mushait, Jazan and Najran. "Pakistan reiterates its unwavering support for the sovereignty, territorial integrity, security and prosperity of the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia, and stands in complete solidarity with the leadership, government and brotherly people of the Kingdom," the statement added. It said the attacks were a "flagrant violation" of Saudi Arabia’s sovereignty and territorial integrity, posing a threat to regional peace and stability while undermining efforts for a peaceful and lasting resolution of the Yemen conflict. The ministry also conveyed its wishes for the swift recovery of those injured in the attacks, adding that Pakistan would continue efforts to promote lasting peace and stability in the region. The Houthis control areas near the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, one of the world’s key shipping routes linking the Red Sea with the Gulf of Aden, giving the group the ability to threaten vital maritime traffic. The strikes had followed growing tensions between the Houthis and Riyadh. After the group threatened further attacks, the Saudi-led coalition supporting Yemen’s internationally recognised government vowed to respond with “unprecedented determination and force” to any attempt to target the kingdom, its citizens or its national assets. Houthi attack on Saudi The flare-up in violence between Saudi Arabia and the group came as tensions mounted between the United States and Iran as the wider Middle East conflict sent oil prices soaring with diplomatic negotiations stalling. Brent crude futures rose $1 to $98/BBL after the Saudi energy ministry statement, while US crude futures rose over $2 to $93.65/BBL. On Monday, the Financial Times newspaper said Aramco's Jazan oil facilities were hit in new strikes, and the damage was being assessed. Reuters was not immediately able to verify the report, and Aramco has not commented. The Houthi military spokesperson said the group would announce in the coming hours a broad operation deep into Saudi territory. "The needed measures will be taken to ensure the safety of the facilities and workers and the continuation of work according to the approved operational plans," said the ministry. Spokesperson Yahya Saree said that Riyadh had taken "escalatory steps" by conducting airstrikes on Yemen, and warned that Houthi strikes would not go unanswered. The Saudi-led coalition did not announce any recent strikes on Yemen, but the Saudi-backed Yemeni government has in recent days mounted an offensive on multiple fronts against the Houthis in Yemen. The coalition vowed to respond firmly to the latest outbreak of hostilities, saying the latest escalation against the de facto OPEC leader was "dangerous". "The coalition will take all necessary operational measures to deter this terrorist militia and resolutely confront its hostile approach," Colonel Turki al-Malki said in a statement on X. The Houthis, who control the most populous parts of Yemen and much of the north, have been launching attacks towards Saudi Arabia since they declared a naval blockade against Riyadh in July, with strikes targeting its vessels in the Red Sea. Makkah Defence Pact The recent Houthi attacks came at a time when Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Türkiye had just formalised their longstanding strategic ties through the signing of the “Makkah Joint Defence Agreement”, a trilateral security framework that its proponents describe as a defensive arrangement aimed at strengthening collective deterrence, enhancing military cooperation and promoting regional stability. The agreement, signed during the Makkah Al-Mukarramah Summit for Joint Defence, has prompted comparisons with military alliances such as NATO. However, according to security analysts, the pact is intended to formalise decades of existing strategic cooperation rather than create a new military bloc or offensive alliance. A formal framework for existing ties According to security analysts, the agreement represents the natural progression of longstanding political, military and strategic relations among the three countries. They note that Pakistan's ties with Turkiye date back to the Khilafat Movement, while Pakistan and Saudi Arabia have maintained decades of defence, political, economic and diplomatic cooperation based on what they describe as mutual trust and shared strategic interests. Rather than establishing an entirely new partnership, analysts say the agreement provides a formal institutional framework for cooperation that has evolved over many years. Security analysts argue that the agreement reflects a rapidly changing regional security environment. They point to regional conflicts, evolving security threats, and changes in the character of modern warfare as factors driving closer strategic coordination among countries that share common security interests. According to them, the trilateral framework is intended to preserve regional stability by strengthening collective security mechanisms instead of relying on ad hoc bilateral cooperation. At its core, the agreement establishes a framework based on the principles of collective security and collective deterrence. Security analysts say its central premise is that aggression against one member would be regarded as a threat to all three, thereby increasing the potential cost of military action and discouraging conflict through credible deterrence. The framework also envisages expanded defence cooperation, including closer military coordination, intelligence sharing, strategic consultations, defence planning and broader institutional cooperation between the three countries. According to analysts, pooling military capabilities and strategic coordination is intended to improve preparedness while reducing the likelihood of regional conflict.

title: Is UCL three-peat really possible for PSG?
author: AFP
description: Luis Enrique's side has already secured back-to-back trophies
text: Luis Enrique's Paris Saint-Germain have already secured their status as one of the Champions League's greatest teams by winning the trophy in back-to-back years, and now they have their sights set on a rare treble. "Doing the treble is the objective, but we know it's going to be very difficult and that there will be obstacles in our way," said PSG captain Marquinhos on the eve of the campaign. After years of disappointment in Europe for the Qatar-owned club, PSG became the real deal after former Barcelona and Spain coach Luis Enrique was appointed in 2023. They reached the semi-finals in his first season, then kicked on following the departure of Kylian Mbappe in 2024. No longer beholden to one or two superstar names, PSG went on to blow the rest of Europe away en route to winning a first Champions League title in 2025 as they destroyed Inter Milan 5-0 in the final. They followed that up by edging Premier League champions Arsenal on penalties in last season's final in Budapest, becoming just the second side to retain the trophy since the inception of the modern Champions League in 1992. But a three-peat at this level would be an achievement on another scale again. Real Madrid did it under Zinedine Zidane, reigning over the continent from 2016 to 2018. Johan Cruyff's Ajax and Franz Beckenbauer's Bayern Munich both won three successive European Cups in the 1970s, while Alfredo Di Stefano's Madrid won five on the bounce at the dawn of the competition between 1956 and 1960. That is the kind of exalted company PSG are hoping to join, but the demands in Europe's elite club competition are now greater than ever -- the new Champions League format led to the Parisians playing a total of 17 games in order to win the trophy in each of the last two campaigns. When at their best, they are utterly thrilling. Their pace in an attack led by Ousmane Dembele and Khvicha Kvaratskhelia is utterly terrifying, and is supported by flying full-backs Achraf Hakimi and Nuno Mendes. Meanwhile their midfield three, led by diminutive Portuguese playmaker Vitinha, can dominate games against far more physical opponents. Luis Enrique: still hungry Hence PSG winning their two titles, and two UEFA Super Cups, despite playing 18 matches against Premier League teams in the last two years. The number of games might be the biggest danger for PSG, who played 121 competitive matches across the last two seasons with a meagre three-week break in between because of the Club World Cup. Either side of that, the majority of their squad were involved in major tournaments in 2024 and have had another shortened summer holiday due to the World Cup. That may explain why they have looked rusty at the beginning of this campaign. However, their margin over the rest of France's top flight is so great that they are still favourites to win Ligue 1 again, even if they choose to regularly rest key players to keep them fresh for the Champions League. Their European campaign could not start with a kinder fixture either, with Slovan Bratislava up first -- things will quickly move up a notch, though, as they visit Manchester City and host Barcelona in October. PSG do not often sell one of their star players but that is what they have done with Bradley Barcola, who joined Liverpool for huge money. Goncalo Ramos, Lee Kang-in and Ibrahim Mbaye, all useful squad options last season, have been sold too. However, Maghnes Akliouche, who played for France at the World Cup, and Ferran Torres -- Spain's final match-winner in North America -- are headline new arrivals. The latter played under Luis Enrique for his country. "He was like a footballing father for me when I played for him in the national team," Torres said after signing from Barcelona. Luis Enrique is the star now, more than any individual player, and he has just signed a new contract to stay in Paris until 2030. "It is the first time I have stayed four years at the same club, and I am more motivated than I was in my first year," he said, insisting that he has lost none of his hunger. That is ominous for PSG's rivals

title: Pakistan eye Asian Games upset
author: Alam Zeb Safi
description: Volleyball side target Japan challenge in the quadrennial event
text: Pakistan’s men’s volleyball team are aiming to defy the odds at the Asian Games in Japan this month, with manager and former captain Naseer Ahmed confident the side can challenge stronger opponents and push for a place in the top eight. Pakistan have been drawn in Group A alongside hosts Japan, Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan in the 16-team competition, which runs from September 26 to October 4. “Yes, I am confident that the team will do well,” Naseer told The Express Tribune in an interview. Pakistan face a daunting opening challenge against world number six Japan, with the South Asian side ranked 38th globally. “No doubt Japan is a much better side but we will try to beat them,” said Naseer, a former Pakistan captain. While Pakistan are unlikely to enter the tournament as medal contenders, Naseer believes the team has enough experience and quality to spring surprises. “Definitely it will be our target to challenge them (Japan). If we fail there then we can beat Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan which will help us move to the top eight,” he said. “Then we will look how we deliver against tough sides in that phase.” Pakistan squad includes a strong core of players who featured at the 2023 Asian Games in Hangzhou, where the team finished fifth. Around nine members of that squad are expected to return for the Japan campaign, while three youngsters have also been included, also comprising an Under-19 setter and a middle blocker. The tournament will provide a major test for Spanish head coach Luis Alberto, who has been working with the national side for the past few months alongside fellow Spaniard Ruiz Pablo, the team’s trainer and conditioning coach. “The boys have been training for four hours daily in two sessions. They have been under training for the last one and a half months,” Naseer said. The team held a training camp at Wah Cantt from August 5 to August 20 before moving to Liaquat Gymnasium, where preparations are continuing. Naseer, who also serves as Director Technical of the Pakistan Volleyball Federation, said the coaching staff had been working intensively to prepare the players for the demanding tournament. “Alberto is a good coach and is working harder on the boys and I hope a better lot will be prepared,” he said. Eighteen players are currently in camp, with the final 12-member squad expected to be announced soon for the trip to Japan. However, preparations have faced a minor facilities concern, with air-conditioning units at Liaquat Gymnasium not yet operational despite having been installed. Although temperatures in Islamabad have begun to ease, running the air-conditioning remains important during intensive training sessions, particularly as players prepare for demanding Asian Games. Pakistan’s best volleyball result in Asian Games history came in 1962, when they won the bronze medal in Jakarta. The team will now attempt to revive some of that competitive spirit. Local coaches Saeed Ahmad and Kashif Maznoor are assisting Alberto during the preparations. Naseer said Pakistan Sports Board would finance 14 members of the squad, while the remaining four would be funded by the Pakistan Volleyball Federation. Group B comprises Iran, Indonesia, Thailand and Kyrgyzstan, while Qatar, India, Vietnam and Hong Kong make up Group C. Group D features Korea, China, Chinese Taipei and the Philippines. For Pakistan, the immediate objective is clear and hat is to compete with Japan, secure victories against Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan, and reach the top eight. With an experienced core, a handful of promising youngsters and a new coaching regime, Naseer believes Pakistan can turn their underdog status into an opportunity.

title: 'You can’t keep brushing things under the rug', says Nadia Hussain on social issues
author: Life And Style Desk
description: Actor argues Pakistan's poverty limits youth-led change seen elsewhere, encourages 'civil' conversation
text: Actor Nadia Hussain took a wide-ranging look at Pakistani society in a recent interview, discussing why she used her platform to weigh in on social issues. Nadia said staying silent was never an option for her. "Some people don't want to talk, but I am not one of those. I feel that because I have a voice and reach people, I want my opinion to reach them. You can't just keep brushing things under the rug," she said. She also credited social media with giving young Pakistanis the confidence earlier generations didn't have. "I think social media has really brought about this change, and I am really happy to see so many youngsters coming up and talking about so many things without fear," the actor said, adding that the platform "has to be used positively, in the right way." The freedom, she cautioned, also came with the responsibility to keep discussions on-topic and civil. "Controlling emotions a little bit, keeping yourself focused on the issue at hand, there is no need to get personal," Nadia said. She added, "Nobody is saying that don't talk about things, but don't cross the line either." Citing India's recent youth-led political movement as proof of what the generation could accomplish when it took the lead, the actor stated, "If any change is to be brought about in our country or any nation, it has to be the younger generation." At the same time, however, she remained candid about the limited access to education which influenced the same kind of mobilisation in Pakistan. "Unfortunately, the problem we have here is poverty. The Gen Z that came out [elsewhere] were not from the poor class; they were middle-class, university and college-going," she said, arguing that the segment of Pakistan's youth with exposure to change remained small. "Poverty is so much that people are more keen on just earning two square meals for their family," Nadia said. She described the cycle as by design rather than accident: "This has been our problem from the beginning: keep the poor poor, keep the illiterate illiterate so they stay busy trapped in their own struggles." Discussing disparity within the entertainment industry in particular, Nadia opened up about the double standards female actors faced as they aged.
